How Much Does One Wrong Answer Cost?
Error Propagation in Constraint Pruning with Noisy LLM Oracles

 

Zhengtao Gui     Weining Shen

University of California, Irvine

Abstract

Constraint pruning saves queries to a large language model (LLM) or another noisy oracle by skipping each yes/no question implied by answers accepted earlier, for example through transitivity. Entity-resolution systems and LLM-based rankers use this idea. However, their analyses typically assume a correct oracle. We argue that pruning should be judged by its risk when the oracle errs, since an accepted wrong answer spreads to every question it implies. When each answer is wrong independently with small probability ε\varepsilon, the first-order risk is set by how many facts one wrong answer corrupts on average. We consider two kinds of constraints. For implication rules, as in taxonomies, pruning in a random order adds no first-order risk: a wrong answer that would change kk facts is accepted with probability 1/k1/k, so it costs one fact on average. Rules with ss premises break this balance: a wrong answer at a premise shared by rr rules can cost order r1−1/sr^{1-1/s} facts. For entity resolution with mm records of one entity, the first-order risk equals ε\varepsilon times the Wiener index (the total pairwise distance) of the spanning tree built by the query order. Pivot orders, which first compare one record with all others, amplify errors by less than 2 and are optimal; random orders by order m1/3m^{1/3}; the common most-similar-first order is the worst in one dimension and, for large mm, worse than random in two. With several entities, the cost of wrongly merging two does not depend on how many others exist. Simulations agree with every predicted constant within sampling error.

1 INTRODUCTION

Constraint pruning reduces the cost of collecting related yes/no facts from an oracle, such as an LLM or a human annotator, whose answers may be wrong. In entity resolution, a system asks whether two records refer to the same entity and skips pairs implied by transitivity (Wang et al., 2013; Vesdapunt et al., 2014). For example, accepting that AA and BB are the same and that BB and CC are the same determines the answer for AA and CC without another query. Similar propagation occurs when enforcing entailment and contradiction constraints between LLM beliefs (Mitchell et al., 2022), skipping comparisons in LLM ranking (Agrawal et al., 2026), or propagating orientation hints in causal discovery (Meek, 1995; Long et al., 2023; Lyu et al., 2026).

However, an accepted error can also propagate to unqueried facts. If AA, BB and CC belong to one entity, a correct “same” answer for A,BA,B followed by a wrong “different” answer for B,CB,C implies a wrong “different” answer for A,CA,C. In the synthetic citation records of Figure 1, one oracle error thus produces two final wrong decisions and saves one query, and the output is still logically consistent. Query counts alone cannot capture this cost. Prior work studies recovery probabilities, assumes deterministic oracles or examines the robustness of query structures (Long et al., 2023; Hiremath et al., 2026; Agrawal et al., 2026; Galhotra et al., 2018).

We study greedy closure decoding: process questions in an order, skip those implied by accepted answers, and otherwise query and accept the oracle’s answer, without revisiting earlier decisions. We measure risk by the expected number of final wrong facts, including inferred ones. The raw baseline asks every question and uses its answer unchanged, without enforcing consistency. Both procedures use the same potential answers: the answers the oracle would give if each question were asked.

In single-error analysis, we make one potential answer wrong and keep all others correct. We count the final wrong facts caused by each error location, averaging over query orders when they are random. In Figure 1, damage is 2; it is 0 if earlier correct answers imply and skip the wrong question. Under independent errors of small probability ε\varepsilon (Long et al., 2023; Hiremath et al., 2026), events with two or more errors have probability O⁡(ε2)O(\varepsilon^{2}) for a fixed finite instance. A reduction lemma expresses risk as ε\varepsilon times the sum of single-error damages, plus O⁡(ε2)O(\varepsilon^{2}). The term linear in ε\varepsilon is the first-order risk; its ratio to the raw baseline’s n​εn\varepsilon is the error amplification, where nn counts questions. Random-order ranking and Meek propagation are not analyzed.

Using single-error analysis, we derive the following first-order risk laws:

  • •

    Risk conservation for pairwise constraints. For every satisfiable 2-CNF theory, including implications and pairwise contradictions, uniformly random orders give mean single-error damage 1 for unfixed facts and 0 for facts fixed by the constraints. Pruning therefore does not increase first-order risk over raw decoding (Section 4).

  • •

    Error amplification through a shared premise. For kk Horn rules with s≥2s\geq 2 premises each and one shared false premise, we derive the exact mean damage of a single wrong answer there, growing as Θ⁡(k1−1/s)\Theta(k^{1-1/s}) under uniformly random orders, for fixed ss (Theorem 6).

  • •

    Relating query order to tree structure. For mm records of one entity, independent errors at a common rate give first-order risk equal to that rate times the noiseless query tree’s Wiener index (total pairwise tree distance). Pivot stars minimize this risk among greedy orders, with amplification below 2; random orders give Θ⁡(m1/3)\Theta(m^{1/3}), and similarity-first can be worse under Theorem 11’s embedding assumptions. We also give bounds for multiple errors at any error rate (Section 5.1).

  • •

    Locality of a single false merge. With only one wrong answer, false-merge damage depends only on the two affected entities. This yields separate within-entity and cross-entity first-order risks. We give bounds, exact small cases and the pivot pipeline’s exact first-order formula; the large-cluster growth exponent remains a conjecture (Section 5.2).

We test the theoretical predictions and compare query orders using simulations and LLM answers on the Cora citation data (Section 6).

2 RELATED WORK

Noisy recovery and tree structure.

Work on probabilistic unclean databases relates integrity constraints to minimum-repair and maximum-likelihood decoding (De Sa et al., 2019; Gilad et al., 2023). Other studies consider noisy graph-label recovery (Globerson et al., 2015; Foster et al., 2018; Heidari et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2022; Jin et al., 2026), correlation clustering (Makarychev et al., 2015), same-cluster queries (Mazumdar and Saha, 2017b) and noisy sorting (Feige et al., 1994; Braverman and Mossel, 2008). Their main goals are query efficiency or global recovery guarantees, usually at constant noise (Banerjee and Shen, 2022). Our tree-based analysis uses Kruskal’s construction (Kruskal, 1956), extremal properties of the Wiener index (Dobrynin et al., 2001), and results on random and spatial spanning trees (Addario-Berry et al., 2009; Addario-Berry et al., 2017; Aizenman et al., 1999).

Entity resolution and LLM comparisons.

Crowdsourced entity resolution uses transitivity (Wang et al., 2013; Vesdapunt et al., 2014). Analyses of query ordering typically assume a correct oracle (Firmani et al., 2016; Mazumdar and Saha, 2017a); robust methods add verification queries (Galhotra et al., 2018) or weaken transitivity (Gruenheid et al., 2015). Recent LLM work studies prompt sensitivity (Gui et al., 2026) and matching errors (Peeters et al., 2025), compares matching strategies (Wang et al., 2025), filters candidates using matching feedback (Chen et al., 2026), and balances quality and cost through operator and model selection (Guo et al., 2026).

Ranking work addresses non-transitive preferences and baseline-sensitive rankings (Xu et al., 2025), presentation-order and transitivity inconsistencies (Zeng et al., 2026), and risks from long inference chains (Agrawal et al., 2026). These studies improve matching, ranking or query allocation. We analyze how an accepted wrong answer causes errors in inferred decisions.

Logical consistency and causal hints.

Belief-correction methods enforce entailment and contradiction relations (Mitchell et al., 2022). Logic.py translates natural-language puzzles into formal problems for a constraint solver (Kesseli et al., 2025). Causal discovery methods elicit and propagate hints about edge orientations (Long et al., 2023; Lyu et al., 2026; Kıcıman et al., 2024), while Guess2Graph uses unreliable expert guesses to order conditional-independence tests (Hiremath et al., 2026). These methods correct answers or select hints. We study a sequential decoding process that accepts oracle answers in order and keeps accepted answers fixed during subsequent inference.

3 SETTING AND REDUCTION LEMMA

Questions, constraints and noisy answers.

There are nn binary questions. Complete vectors satisfying the constraints form the code 𝒞⊆{0,1}n\mathcal{C}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n}; each is a feasible codeword. They are the models (satisfying assignments) of a propositional theory Φ\Phi. The decoder knows the constraints but not the fixed truth x⋆∈𝒞x^{\star}\in\mathcal{C}. We study implication, 2-CNF and definite Horn theories (Section 4), partitions under “same entity” transitivity (Section 5), and total orders under “before” transitivity (Section A.4).

The oracle’s potential answer yiy_{i} to question ii is observed only if queried. Thus y=x⋆⊕Zy=x^{\star}\oplus Z, where ZiZ_{i} are independent Bern⁡(ε)\mathrm{Bern}(\varepsilon) variables: Zi=1Z_{i}=1 flips the true answer and Zi=0Z_{i}=0 leaves it unchanged. Section 5.2 allows two rates. Hamming loss dH​(x^,x⋆)d_{\mathrm{H}}(\hat{x},x^{\star}) counts wrong final answers, including inferred ones; risk R⁡(ε)=𝔼​dH​(x^,x⋆)R(\varepsilon)=\mathbb{E}\,d_{\mathrm{H}}(\hat{x},x^{\star}) is its expectation. The raw decoder asks all questions and returns yy, with risk Rraw=ε​nR_{\mathrm{raw}}=\varepsilon n; the output may violate constraints.

The greedy decoder GπG_{\pi} follows order π\pi, storing accepted question–answer pairs in an initially empty set LL. Among codewords agreeing with LL, if all give the same answer at ii, use it and skip the query. Otherwise both answers are feasible: query the oracle and add (i,yi)(i,y_{i}) to LL, keeping this answer fixed. A wrong answer can thus be accepted while preserving feasibility. After all questions, one codeword remains (Lemma 16), also obtained by the accept-if-consistent rule. Unless stated otherwise, π\pi is uniform and independent of ZZ. Implication tests take polynomial time without enumerating 𝒞\mathcal{C}: satisfiability tests for 2-CNF and Horn theories, union-find for partitions and transitive closure for orders. The maximum-likelihood (ML) decoder uses all answers jointly, returning a codeword closest to yy in Hamming distance, with uniform tie-breaking.

Single-error damage.

For a decoder x^\hat{x} whose output depends on yy and on an independent seed π\pi, the single-error damage at question aa is the expected loss when only the answer to aa is wrong,

D⁡(a)=𝔼π​dH​(x^​(x⋆⊕ea,π),x⋆),D(a)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\,d_{\mathrm{H}}\big(\hat{x}(x^{\star}\oplus e_{a},\pi),\,x^{\star}\big),

where eae_{a} is the aa-th unit vector. For the greedy decoder we write Dπ​(a)=dH​(Gπ​(x⋆⊕ea),x⋆)D_{\pi}(a)=d_{\mathrm{H}}(G_{\pi}(x^{\star}\oplus e_{a}),x^{\star}) for a fixed order, so that D⁡(a)=𝔼π​Dπ​(a)D(a)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}D_{\pi}(a). The first-order constant is κ=limε→0R⁡(ε)/ε\kappa=\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}R(\varepsilon)/\varepsilon, and the amplification of a decoder is κ/κraw=κ/n\kappa/\kappa_{\rm raw}=\kappa/n, the mean damage of one wrong answer relative to the raw decoder.

For x∈𝒞x\in\mathcal{C} let ma​(x)m_{a}(x) be the number of codewords of the form x⊕ea⊕ebx\oplus e_{a}\oplus e_{b}, b≠ab\neq a, when x⊕ea∉𝒞x\oplus e_{a}\notin\mathcal{C} (and 00 otherwise). In that case they are the codewords other than xx that tie with xx as nearest to x⊕eax\oplus e_{a}.

Lemma 1 (Reduction lemma).

Let x^\hat{x} be any decoder that returns x⋆x^{\star} when there is no wrong answer. For every ε∈[0,12]\varepsilon\in[0,\tfrac{1}{2}],

|Rx^​(ε)−ε​∑a=1nD⁡(a)|≤32​ε2​n2​(n−1).\Big|R_{\hat{x}}(\varepsilon)-\varepsilon\sum_{a=1}^{n}D(a)\Big|\leq\tfrac{3}{2}\,\varepsilon^{2}n^{2}(n-1).

Moreover: (i) ML has DML​(a)=1D_{\rm ML}(a)=1 if x⋆⊕ea∈𝒞x^{\star}\oplus e_{a}\in\mathcal{C} and DML​(a)=2​ma/(1+ma)D_{\rm ML}(a)=2m_{a}/(1+m_{a}) otherwise. (ii) The greedy decoder has first-order constant ∑a𝔼π​Dπ​(a)\sum_{a}\mathbb{E}_{\pi}D_{\pi}(a), so its amplification is the mean damage of one wrong answer.

The remainder grows with nn, so the expansion describes a fixed instance as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0.

4 IMPLICATION THEORIES AND HORN RULES

We apply the single-error analysis of Section 3 to logical rules to identify when constraint propagation amplifies errors. We first show that, under uniformly random query orders, implication rules and, more generally, 2-CNF constraints do not increase first-order risk over raw decoding; a shared-premise Horn family then shows why this conclusion does not hold in general.

Let Φ\Phi be a satisfiable theory over atoms VV, |V|=n|V|=n, each representing a binary fact. Write the truth x⋆x^{\star} as a satisfying assignment σ⋆\sigma^{\star} here. A literal is an atom or its negation. Let tx=xt_{x}=x when σ⋆​(x)=1\sigma^{\star}(x)=1 and tx=¬xt_{x}=\neg x otherwise, with t¯x\bar{t}_{x} the opposite literal. The backbone B={x:Φ⊧tx}B=\{x:\Phi\models t_{x}\} contains facts fixed by the rules (⊧\models denotes logical entailment). For a∉Ba\notin B, the flip set

Ka={x∈V:Φ∧t¯a⊧t¯x}K_{a}=\{x\in V:\ \Phi\wedge\bar{t}_{a}\models\bar{t}_{x}\}

contains aa and every atom whose value is forced to change by a wrong value at aa. We say that aa has the single-flip property if flipping exactly the atoms of KaK_{a} in σ⋆\sigma^{\star}, while leaving all others unchanged, gives another model of Φ\Phi.

Theorem 2 (Damage of one wrong answer).

Suppose that the only wrong answer is at atom aa. If a∈Ba\in B, the greedy decoder returns the truth for every order. If a∉Ba\notin B has the single-flip property, then for every order π\pi

Dπ​(a)=|Ka|⋅𝟏​{a​ comes first in ​π​ among ​Ka},D_{\pi}(a)=|K_{a}|\cdot\mathbf{1}\{a\text{ comes first in }\pi\text{ among }K_{a}\},

so 𝔼π​Dπ​(a)=1\mathbb{E}_{\pi}D_{\pi}(a)=1 for a uniformly random (or any exchangeable) order.

In the second case, a correct value on another atom of KaK_{a} implies aa’s true value and skips its query. Only if aa comes first is the error accepted, causing |Ka||K_{a}| wrong facts. Its probability 1/|Ka|1/|K_{a}| yields mean damage 1; individual runs have damage 0 or |Ka||K_{a}|.

Proposition 3.

If every clause of Φ\Phi has at most two literals, every atom outside the backbone has the single-flip property.

Proposition 3 holds because, if a flip makes one literal of a two-literal clause false, Φ∧t¯a\Phi\wedge\bar{t}_{a} forces the other to be true, preserving the clause.

Corollary 4 (Conservation law).

Let Φ\Phi be a satisfiable 2-CNF theory with backbone BB. For every ε∈[0,12]\varepsilon\in[0,\tfrac{1}{2}],

−ε2​n​(n−1)≤Rgr​(ε)−ε⁡(n−|B|)≤12​ε2​n2​(n−1).-\varepsilon^{2}n(n-1)\ \leq\ R_{\mathrm{gr}}(\varepsilon)-\varepsilon\,(n-|B|)\ \leq\ \tfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon^{2}n^{2}(n-1).

In particular, for every implication graph G=(V,A)G=(V,A), with ΦG=⋀(u,v)∈A(¬u∨v)\Phi_{G}=\bigwedge_{(u,v)\in A}(\neg u\vee v), greedy decoding has Rgr​(ε)=ε​n+O⁡(ε2)=Rraw​(ε)+O⁡(ε2)R_{\mathrm{gr}}(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon n+O(\varepsilon^{2})=R_{\mathrm{raw}}(\varepsilon)+O(\varepsilon^{2}), for false-positive and false-negative errors alike and for every truth.

Thus the first-order risk is ε⁡(n−|B|)\varepsilon(n-|B|); implication graphs have no fixed facts and match raw at first order. Multiple errors can still cause differences. If accepted, a false positive (false to true) changes false descendants, and a false negative (true to false) changes true ancestors. The order matters: on v1→…→vnv_{1}\to\dots\to v_{n} queried as v1,…,vnv_{1},\dots,v_{n}, a single false positive is accepted and changes every later false fact.

Proposition 5 (ML on 2-CNF).

On a satisfiable 2-CNF theory, the ML single-error damage at a∉Ba\notin B is 1 if |Ka|≤2|K_{a}|\leq 2 and 0 if |Ka|≥3|K_{a}|\geq 3. Hence RML​(ε)=Rgr​(ε)−ε​#​{a∉B:|Ka|≥3}+O⁡(ε2)R_{\mathrm{ML}}(\varepsilon)=R_{\mathrm{gr}}(\varepsilon)-\varepsilon\,\#\{a\notin B:|K_{a}|\geq 3\}+O(\varepsilon^{2}).

Horn rules.

The Horn hub Hk,sH_{k,s} has kk rules bi,1∧⋯∧bi,s−1∧a→cib_{i,1}\wedge\dots\wedge b_{i,s-1}\wedge a\to c_{i} (i=1,…,ki=1,\dots,k), sharing premise aa. Each rule’s other premises and conclusion occur in no other rule. All bi,jb_{i,j} are true and a,cia,c_{i} are false, so n=1+k​sn=1+ks. For s=2s=2 this is the pattern isa⁡(x,y)∧has⁡(y,z)→has⁡(x,z)\mathrm{isa}(x,y)\wedge\mathrm{has}(y,z)\to\mathrm{has}(x,z) with a shared premise.

Theorem 6 (Horn hub).

For a single false positive at the shared premise aa of Hk,sH_{k,s}, s≥2s\geq 2, and a uniformly random order,

𝔼π​Dπ​(a)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\pi}D_{\pi}(a) =(k+1)​∫01(1−us)k​𝑑u\displaystyle=(k+1)\int_{0}^{1}(1-u^{s})^{k}\,du
=(k+1)​Γ​(1+1s)​Γ​(k+1)Γ⁡(k+1+1s),\displaystyle=\frac{(k+1)\,\Gamma(1+\frac{1}{s})\,\Gamma(k+1)}{\Gamma(k+1+\frac{1}{s})},

which equals Γ⁡(1+1s)​k1−1/s​(1+O⁡(1/k))\Gamma(1+\frac{1}{s})\,k^{1-1/s}(1+O(1/k)). Every other single error on Hk,sH_{k,s} has damage exactly 1. Hence Rgr​(ε)=Rraw​(ε)+ε⁡[𝔼π​Dπ​(a)−1]+O⁡(ε2)R_{\mathrm{gr}}(\varepsilon)=R_{\mathrm{raw}}(\varepsilon)+\varepsilon\,[\mathbb{E}_{\pi}D_{\pi}(a)-1]+O(\varepsilon^{2}).

Here Γ\Gamma is the Gamma function. The mechanism differs from Theorem 2: a wrong aa alone implies no other values. It is skipped only if one rule’s other ss atoms were processed earlier: their true premises and false conclusion force aa false. If accepted, each rule’s last atom is inferred wrongly and skipped; it can be a premise or the conclusion. Including aa, the total damage is k+1k+1.

Appendix A.2 gives the ML proof and the arrival-time derivation of the Horn formula, including its s=2s=2 special case.

For Horn theories with at most ss premises per rule, we conjecture that mean false-positive damage at aa is bounded by Cs​c1−1/sC_{s}\,c^{1-1/s}, where cc counts newly true atoms after adding aa to the truth, including aa (Conjecture 19). The hub shows this exponent cannot be lowered.

Under uniformly random query orders, acceptance probability and propagation damage balance for 2-CNF constraints, so pruning does not increase first-order risk over raw decoding. The shared-premise Horn family shows that this balance can fail, with the mean cost of one wrong answer growing with the number of rules.

5 ENTITY RESOLUTION WITH TRANSITIVITY PRUNING

We now apply the greedy-decoding framework to entity resolution, where each pairwise answer states whether two records refer to the same entity. Transitivity lets “same” on AA–BB and BB–CC imply “same” on AA–CC, saving a query but potentially spreading an error. This involves three pairwise facts, so the 2-CNF conservation law in Section 4 does not directly apply. We first study false splits within one entity, then false merges between entities.

5.1 One Cluster

The mm records in [m][m] all refer to one entity, so every pair’s true answer is “same”. The algorithm does not know this: its feasible outputs are all partitions of [m][m], each specifying which records belong together. There are (m2)\binom{m}{2} pairwise questions. We write the error rate as δ\delta: each answer is independently flipped to “different” with probability δ\delta. The loss LπL_{\pi} counts pairs incorrectly separated in the final output.

The union-find pipeline UπU_{\pi} (Wang et al., 2013) maintains current groups of records, called blocks, and accepted “≠\neq” constraints between them. A block need not coincide with a true entity. It scans pairs in order π\pi. For {u,v}\{u,v\}, membership in one block already implies “same”, while a ≠\neq constraint between their blocks implies “different”; either case skips the query. Otherwise it asks the oracle: “same” merges the blocks, and “different” records a constraint. Existing constraints are carried over when blocks merge. Lemma 20 shows that this is the greedy decoder on the partition code.

Construct the Kruskal tree TπT_{\pi} from the order alone, without using the noisy answers. Scan pairs in order π\pi, retaining a pair only when it connects two components of the edges retained so far. With all answers correct, these m−1m-1 tree edges are exactly the queried pairs. For a tree TT, let dT​(u,v)d_{T}(u,v) count edges on the unique path from uu to vv. Its Wiener index (Wiener, 1947) is

W⁡(T)=∑{u,v}dT​(u,v)=∑e∈Tne​(m−ne)W(T)=\sum_{\{u,v\}}d_{T}(u,v)=\sum_{e\in T}n_{e}(m-n_{e})

where deleting edge ee splits the tree into parts of sizes nen_{e} and m−nem-n_{e}. Exactly ne​(m−ne)n_{e}(m-n_{e}) pairwise paths use that edge, which gives the second equality.

Lemma 7 (Sandwich).

Fix any order π\pi and any pattern of wrong answers. For a pair {u,v}\{u,v\}, let k⁡(u,v)k(u,v) be the number of edges of TπT_{\pi} whose answer is wrong on the tree path from uu to vv. If k⁡(u,v)=0k(u,v)=0, then uu and vv end in the same block; if k⁡(u,v)=1k(u,v)=1, they end in different blocks. Hence N1≤Lπ≤N≥1N_{1}\leq L_{\pi}\leq N_{\geq 1}, where NjN_{j} (N≥jN_{\geq j}) is the number of pairs with k=jk=j (k≥jk\geq j).

Every tree edge is queried even when errors occur, and each pipeline block stays inside a component of the forest built so far by the Kruskal scan. This yields Lemma 7. Paths with two or more wrong edges need not lead to separation; with a single wrong answer, the two bounds coincide and give the exact loss.

Theorem 8 (Wiener law).

For every order π\pi and every δ∈[0,1]\delta\in[0,1],

δ​W​(Tπ)−δ2​W2​(Tπ)≤𝔼​Lπ≤δ​W​(Tπ),\delta W(T_{\pi})-\delta^{2}W_{2}(T_{\pi})\ \leq\ \mathbb{E}L_{\pi}\ \leq\ \delta W(T_{\pi}),

where W2​(T)=∑{u,v}dT​(u,v)2W_{2}(T)=\sum_{\{u,v\}}d_{T}(u,v)^{2}. A single wrong answer on a tree edge ee costs exactly ne​(m−ne)n_{e}(m-n_{e}) pairs, and a single wrong answer on any other pair costs nothing.

Theorem 8 makes the effect of the query tree explicit: for fixed mm, 𝔼​Lπ=δ​W​(Tπ)+O⁡(δ2)\mathbb{E}L_{\pi}=\delta W(T_{\pi})+O(\delta^{2}) as δ→0\delta\to 0, with the displayed bounds valid for every δ∈[0,1]\delta\in[0,1]. Raw decoding has risk δ​(m2)\delta\binom{m}{2}, so first-order amplification is W⁡(Tπ)/(m2)W(T_{\pi})/\binom{m}{2}, the average tree distance. The single-error cut identity and Lemma 7 hold for any error placement; the expectation uses independent errors with a common rate. Galhotra et al. (2018) previously identified the vulnerability of tree-based inference to errors; here the bounds quantify it for this decoder.

Proposition 9 (Pivot orders are optimal).

(i) For every spanning tree TT of KmK_{m}, m≥3m\geq 3, W⁡(T)≥(m−1)2W(T)\geq(m-1)^{2}, with equality if and only if TT is a star (a classical property of the Wiener index; Dobrynin et al., 2001). So the first-order risk δ​W​(Tπ)\delta W(T_{\pi}) is minimized exactly by the orders whose Kruskal tree is a star, such as asking every pair with a fixed pivot first (Vesdapunt et al., 2014); their amplification is 2​(m−1)/m<22(m-1)/m<2. (ii) Among decoders that observe the answers on a fixed spanning tree TT only (non-adaptive designs with m−1m-1 queries, each observed answer flipped independently with probability δ\delta), if δ≤1/m\delta\leq 1/m the worst-case risk over the one-cluster truth and the m−1m-1 two-block partitions obtained by cutting one edge of TT is at least 12​δ​(1−δ)m−2​(m−1)2\frac{1}{2}\delta(1-\delta)^{m-2}(m-1)^{2}. So, to first order in δ\delta, the worst-case risk of every such design is at least half of the pivot order’s risk δ​(m−1)2\delta(m-1)^{2} at the one-cluster truth.

Proposition 10 (Random order).

For a uniformly random order, TπT_{\pi} is the minimum spanning tree MSTm\mathrm{MST}_{m} of KmK_{m} with i.i.d. weights, and 𝔼​L=δ​𝔼​W​(MSTm)+O⁡(δ2)\mathbb{E}L=\delta\,\mathbb{E}\,W(\mathrm{MST}_{m})+O(\delta^{2}) with 𝔼​W​(MSTm)=Θ⁡(m7/3)\mathbb{E}\,W(\mathrm{MST}_{m})=\Theta(m^{7/3}), an amplification Θ⁡(m1/3)\Theta(m^{1/3}). At δ=xm−1/3\delta=x\,m^{-1/3} with x>0x>0 fixed, the expected fraction of lost pairs stays bounded away from 0 and 1 as m→∞m\to\infty.

Independent uniform edge weights generate a uniform pair order; known tree-distance estimates (Addario-Berry et al., 2009; Addario-Berry et al., 2017) then yield Proposition 10 through Lemma 7.

Theorem 11 (Most-similar-first order).

Let items carry i.i.d. embeddings on [0,1]d[0,1]^{d} with a density bounded below by f0>0f_{0}>0, let μf\mu_{f} be the mean distance between two items, and let pairs be asked in increasing order of distance. Then TπT_{\pi} is the Euclidean minimum spanning tree, and for every m≥2m\geq 2 with f0​m≥2​log⁡mf_{0}m\geq 2\log m (natural logarithm),

𝔼​W​(EMSTm)(m2)≥μf−d/m4​d​(f0​m2​log⁡m)1/d.\frac{\mathbb{E}\,W(\mathrm{EMST}_{m})}{\binom{m}{2}}\ \geq\ \frac{\mu_{f}-\sqrt{d}/m}{4\sqrt{d}}\Big(\frac{f_{0}\,m}{2\log m}\Big)^{1/d}.

For d=1d=1 the amplification is exactly (m+1)/3(m+1)/3.

Under these embedding assumptions, similarity-first has larger asymptotic amplification than random order in one and two dimensions. Nearby connections can create long tree paths, giving a single error more opportunities to separate a pair. In one dimension, the tree is a path, which maximizes the Wiener index (Dobrynin et al., 2001). Appendix A.3 derives the tree estimates and quantitative growth-rate comparisons. With unequal error rates, semantic similarity-based querying (Wang et al., 2013) also depends on which pairs are answered wrongly (Section 6).

5.2 Several Clusters

Now records belong to KK true clusters of sizes s1,…,sKs_{1},\dots,s_{K}, with n=∑isin=\sum_{i}s_{i} records (here nn counts records, not pairwise facts). All (n2)\binom{n}{2} pairs are scanned in a uniformly random order. Answers are flipped independently: a within-cluster pair is wrongly answered “different” with probability εw\varepsilon_{w}, and a cross-cluster pair “same” with probability εx\varepsilon_{x}. Write RUR_{U} for the expected number of wrong final pair decisions, counting both false merges and false splits.

To isolate a false merge, consider only two clusters of sizes sA,sBs_{A},s_{B}. Fix a cross pair and make its potential answer “same”, with all other answers correct. Let g⁡(sA,sB)g(s_{A},s_{B}) be its mean damage over random orders, counting a skipped wrong answer as zero, and write g⁡(s)=g⁡(s,s)g(s)=g(s,s). Accepting the error can also block later correct within-cluster merges. Thus gg includes both wrong cross-cluster merges and possible splits within these two clusters.

Theorem 12 (Exact first-order decomposition).

With ε=max⁡(εw,εx)\varepsilon=\max(\varepsilon_{w},\varepsilon_{x}),

RU=\displaystyle R_{U}={} εw​∑i=1K𝔼​W​(MSTsi)\displaystyle\varepsilon_{w}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\,W(\mathrm{MST}_{s_{i}})
+εx∑i<jsisjg(si,sj)+O(ε2).\displaystyle+\varepsilon_{x}\sum_{i<j}s_{i}s_{j}\,g(s_{i},s_{j})+O(\varepsilon^{2}).

In particular the damage of a false merge does not depend on KK or on the other clusters.

The first term sums false-split risks within the true clusters, applying the Wiener law to each. The second sums false-merge risks: clusters i,ji,j have si​sjs_{i}s_{j} cross pairs, each contributing mean damage g⁡(si,sj)g(s_{i},s_{j}). Correct cross-cluster answers confine a single error to its incident clusters. Simultaneous errors can involve more clusters, so this locality underlies the first-order decomposition.

The following bounds on g⁡(s)g(s) count skipped errors as zero.

Proposition 13 (Size of one false merge).

Let qq be the event that the false pair is asked. For s≥2s\geq 2, 12​s−1≤ℙ⁡(q)≤12.4s+1+12​(916)s−1\frac{1}{2s-1}\leq\mathbb{P}(q)\leq\frac{12.4}{s+1}+\frac{1}{2}\big(\frac{9}{16}\big)^{s-1} and s−12​s−1≤g⁡(s)≤13​s\frac{s-1}{2s-1}\leq g(s)\leq 13\,s. Under standard local-limit facts for Erdős–Rényi graphs, s​ℙ​(q)→Cq≈1.4286s\,\mathbb{P}(q)\to C_{q}\approx 1.4286 (Proposition 23).

Exact computation gives g⁡(2)=29/18g(2)=29/18 and g⁡(3)=313913/150150≈2.091g(3)=313913/150150\approx 2.091 (Table 5). For comparison, the pivot pipeline processes records one at a time. It compares each new record with the first record of each existing block, in block-creation order, until “same” lets it join that block; if all answers are “different”, it creates a new block (Vesdapunt et al., 2014). Its first-order risk is given by Proposition 14.

Proposition 14 (Pivot pipeline).

For KK clusters of size ss, with items arriving in a uniformly random order,

Rpiv=εw​K​(s−1)2+εx​(K2)​s​(2​s−1)+O⁡(ε2).R_{\rm piv}=\varepsilon_{w}K(s-1)^{2}+\varepsilon_{x}\binom{K}{2}s(2s-1)+O(\varepsilon^{2}).

The coefficient of εx\varepsilon_{x} in Proposition 14, divided by the (K2)​s2\binom{K}{2}s^{2} cross pairs, gives mean damage (2​s−1)/s(2s-1)/s per potential wrong cross-pair answer. The random-order mean is g⁡(s)g(s), giving a loss ratio g⁡(s)​s/(2​s−1)g(s)\,s/(2s-1).

Conjecture 15 (Contamination law).

g⁡(s)=Θ⁡(s2/3)g(s)=\Theta(s^{2/3}). Consequently, for K≥2K\geq 2 clusters of size ss, RU=Θ⁡(εw​K​s7/3)+Θ⁡(εx​K2​s8/3)R_{U}=\Theta(\varepsilon_{w}Ks^{7/3})+\Theta(\varepsilon_{x}K^{2}s^{8/3}) at first order.

Simulation supports s2/3s^{2/3} growth but does not determine the asymptotic constant (Figure 2, lower panel C; Table 6). A proof would need a scaling limit describing the constrained merging process in the critical window of the within-cluster random graphs.

In entity resolution, the noiseless query tree determines one-cluster first-order risk; with independent errors at a common rate, pivot stars minimize this risk among greedy query orders. With several entities, a single error remains confined to the one or two entities involved, yielding separate first-order contributions from within-entity and cross-entity errors.

6 EXPERIMENTAL VALIDATION

We check the formulas in simulation, compare query orders at higher error rates allowing multiple wrong answers, and evaluate final losses using LLM answers on Cora. Loss counts wrong final decisions, including inferred ones. In record matching, false splits separate records of the same entity, while false merges group records of different entities. Amplification is the final wrong-pair count divided by the raw baseline’s wrong-answer count. All single-error averages count skipped errors as zero.

Figure 2 connects the propagation examples with numerical checks of the preceding laws. (A) contrasts 2-CNF conservation with shared-premise Horn amplification. In (B), splitting eight records into 1+71+7 or 4+44+4 produces 7 or 16 wrong pairs. Its lower panel compares first-order amplification, equal to mean noiseless-tree distance under independent, equal-rate errors. In (C), one false merge can cause both false merges and false splits within the two involved entities; the lower panel compares g⁡(s)g(s) with pivot’s (2​s−1)/s(2s-1)/s. The 2.38​m1/32.38m^{1/3} and 0.9​s2/30.9s^{2/3} curves are guides; the finite-size slope ≈0.43\approx 0.43 in (B) does not determine the asymptotic exponent, and (C) does not establish its asymptotic constant.

Checking the analytical predictions.

Enumeration and direct decoding test conservation, Horn damage and false-merge locality independently of the formulas. The conservation estimates are within 2.66 Monte Carlo standard errors (MCSE) of their predictions; the other tabulated estimates are within 1.62 MCSE. At ε=10−3\varepsilon=10^{-3}, dividing the full decoder’s mean false-merge (FP) and false-split (FN) counts by ε\varepsilon also gives estimates close to the first-order coefficients. Appendix B gives the full comparison (Table 4), simulation settings and statistical details.

Higher error rates.

We also test the full decoder where multiple errors may interact. One entity has m=100m=100 records, so every pair’s correct answer is “same”. Each answer is independently flipped to “different” at rate δ=1%\delta=1\%–20%20\%, with 200 runs per configuration. Table 2 reports the fraction of pairs wrongly separated: at a 10% answer-error rate, this fraction averages 17.4% for pivot and 45.8% for random order. Across the tested rates, random-order mean loss is 1.81.8–4.34.3 times the pivot value; at m=200m=200 the ratios are 1.91.9–5.45.4 (Table 7). Pivot’s advantage therefore persists in these settings. At higher rates, the first-order sum overestimates random-order loss: several errors may affect the same pairs, which are counted only once.

Real LLM answers.

In Cora (Hasso Plattner Institute, n.d.), each entity comprises citation records of one paper. We use 62,423 within-entity pairs from 23 entities with at least 20 records. Qwen2.5-1.5B (base) (Qwen Team, 2024) answers 6.6% wrongly. All orders reuse cached answers; similarity-first follows decreasing textual similarity.

Pivot loses less than random order, while similarity-first has the lowest point estimate (Table 3). Pooled answer-error rates on noiseless query-tree edges are 2.2% for similarity-first, 8.4% for pivot and 8.6% for random order, linking loss to both tree shape and edge accuracy. Pivot beats random order at all tested thresholds (approximately 1%–20% answer-error rates; Table 8).

Redistributing each entity’s errors uniformly, with error counts fixed and query orders matched, raises all three losses and removes similarity-first’s advantage over pivot (Table 3, rows 2–3). Thus error locations matter.

In six blocks of three or four similar entities, both false merges and false splits can occur; pivot has the lowest pooled loss. Appendix C gives the prompting protocol, threshold sweep and detailed results for these settings.

7 DISCUSSION

We analyzed error propagation in greedy, constraint-based decoding. Under uniformly random query orders, 2-CNF constraints do not increase first-order risk over raw answers, while shared-premise Horn rules can amplify errors. In record matching, one-entity first-order risk is determined by pairwise distances on the noiseless query tree. Under independent, equal-rate errors, pivot minimizes this risk among greedy orders. With one wrong answer, false merges affect only two entities. Simulations support the formulas and show pivot’s advantage over random order at the tested higher error rates. The Cora results show that tree shape and error locations both matter: uniformly redistributing errors removes similarity-first’s advantage over pivot. Future work could study interacting errors, especially false merges, across more models and datasets. The general Horn false-positive damage bound and false-merge growth law remain conjectures.

How Much Does One Wrong Answer Cost?
Supplementary Materials

 

Appendix A Proofs

A.1 Setting and reduction

We first express small-noise risk in terms of single-error damage, then prove the results for logical constraints, entity resolution and sorting. Numerical checks are in Section B.

A code is a finite nonempty set 𝒞⊆{0,1}n\mathcal{C}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n}. Its elements are codewords, and its nn positions are coordinates (the binary queries). The truth is a codeword x⋆∈𝒞x^{\star}\in\mathcal{C}. The answers are y=x⋆⊕Zy=x^{\star}\oplus Z, where Z1,…,ZnZ_{1},\dots,Z_{n} are independent and Zi∼Bern⁡(ε)Z_{i}\sim\mathrm{Bern}(\varepsilon) with ε∈[0,12]\varepsilon\in[0,\tfrac{1}{2}]. We write eae_{a} for the aa-th unit vector of {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n} and dHd_{\mathrm{H}} for the Hamming distance. A decoder maps the answers yy to an estimate, possibly using a random seed π\pi independent of ZZ to choose the query order or break ties; its output is x^\hat{x}. Its risk is R⁡(ε)=𝔼​dH​(x^,x⋆)R(\varepsilon)=\mathbb{E}\,d_{\mathrm{H}}(\hat{x},x^{\star}), where the expectation is over ZZ and π\pi. We use three decoders.

  • •

    The raw decoder outputs x^=y\hat{x}=y. Hence Rraw​(ε)=ε​nR_{\mathrm{raw}}(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon n exactly.

  • •

    The ML decoder outputs a codeword at minimum Hamming distance from yy, with ties broken uniformly at random. For ε<12\varepsilon<\tfrac{1}{2} this is maximum-likelihood decoding.

  • •

    The greedy decoder GπG_{\pi} processes the coordinates in an order π\pi. It starts from the empty set L0=∅L_{0}=\emptyset of accepted answers. At step tt, with i=π⁡(t)i=\pi(t), it skips ii if all codewords consistent with Lt−1L_{t-1} have the same value at ii (the query is implied); otherwise it accepts the answer and sets Lt=Lt−1∪{(i,yi)}L_{t}=L_{t-1}\cup\{(i,y_{i})\}. It outputs the unique codeword consistent with LnL_{n}. Lemma 16 in Section A.2 shows that this codeword exists and is unique. Unless stated otherwise, π\pi is uniform over the n!n! orders and independent of ZZ.

For a codeword xx and a coordinate aa we define

Ba(x)={b≠a:x⊕ea∉𝒞,x⊕ea⊕eb∈𝒞},ma(x)=|Ba(x)|.B_{a}(x)=\{b\neq a:\ x\oplus e_{a}\notin\mathcal{C},\ x\oplus e_{a}\oplus e_{b}\in\mathcal{C}\},\qquad m_{a}(x)=|B_{a}(x)|.

If ma​(x)≥1m_{a}(x)\geq 1, an error at aa leaves the observed word at distance 1 from xx and from ma​(x)m_{a}(x) alternative codewords. Each alternative differs from the original codeword in two positions and is therefore at distance 2 from xx. For a decoder with seed π\pi, the single-error damage at aa is the expected loss when the only wrong answer is at aa:

D⁡(a)=𝔼π​dH​(x^​(x⋆⊕ea,π),x⋆).D(a)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\,d_{\mathrm{H}}\big(\hat{x}(x^{\star}\oplus e_{a},\pi),\,x^{\star}\big).

Probabilistic unclean databases (De Sa et al., 2019) formalize a noisy-channel model of database cleaning and seek the most likely intended database. Their Theorems 7 and 8 relate this optimum to weighted minimum repairs under sufficiently high constraint weights and specified prior/channel assumptions; the update-repair result also requires attribute independence. Union-bound analyses of ML decoding are surveyed by Sason and Shamai (2006); part (i) of Lemma 1 gives an elementary first-order expansion for our finite code setting. Part (ii) applies the same reduction to greedy decoding.

Proof of Lemma 1, remainder bound.

We show that every decoder that is exact on the noiseless input, that is, x^​(x⋆,π)=x⋆\hat{x}(x^{\star},\pi)=x^{\star} for every seed, satisfies for all ε∈[0,12]\varepsilon\in[0,\tfrac{1}{2}]

|R⁡(ε)−ε​∑a=1nD⁡(a)|≤ε2​n​(n−1)​(maxa⁡D⁡(a)+n2)≤32​ε2​n2​(n−1).\Big|\,R(\varepsilon)-\varepsilon\sum_{a=1}^{n}D(a)\,\Big|\ \leq\ \varepsilon^{2}\,n(n-1)\Big(\max_{a}D(a)+\frac{n}{2}\Big)\ \leq\ \tfrac{3}{2}\,\varepsilon^{2}n^{2}(n-1). (1)

If |S|≥2|S|\geq 2, the loss lies in [0,n][0,n], and a union bound over pairs of coordinates gives ℙ⁡(|S|≥2)≤(n2)​ε2\mathbb{P}(|S|\geq 2)\leq\binom{n}{2}\varepsilon^{2}. Therefore

R(ε)−ε∑aD(a)=−ε[1−(1−ε)n−1]∑aD(a)+r,0≤r≤12n2(n−1)ε2.R(\varepsilon)-\varepsilon\sum_{a}D(a)\ =\ -\varepsilon\,\big[1-(1-\varepsilon)^{n-1}\big]\sum_{a}D(a)\ +\ r,\qquad 0\leq r\leq\tfrac{1}{2}\,n^{2}(n-1)\,\varepsilon^{2}.

Bernoulli’s inequality gives 0≤1−(1−ε)n−1≤(n−1)​ε0\leq 1-(1-\varepsilon)^{n-1}\leq(n-1)\varepsilon. So the first term lies in [−ε2​n​(n−1)​maxa⁡D⁡(a), 0][-\varepsilon^{2}n(n-1)\max_{a}D(a),\,0], and the first inequality in (1) follows. The second inequality follows from D⁡(a)≤nD(a)\leq n. The same argument applies when coordinate ii has its own error rate εi≤ε\varepsilon_{i}\leq\varepsilon. Proof of Lemma 1(i).

We show that the ML decoder has DML​(a)=1D_{\mathrm{ML}}(a)=1 if x⋆⊕ea∈𝒞x^{\star}\oplus e_{a}\in\mathcal{C} and DML​(a)=2​ma​(x⋆)/(1+ma​(x⋆))D_{\mathrm{ML}}(a)=2m_{a}(x^{\star})/(1+m_{a}(x^{\star})) otherwise, so that

RML(ε)=ε[N1(x⋆)+∑a:x⋆⊕ea∉𝒞2​ma​(x⋆)1+ma​(x⋆)]+O(ε2).R_{\mathrm{ML}}(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon\Big[N_{1}(x^{\star})+\sum_{a:\,x^{\star}\oplus e_{a}\notin\mathcal{C}}\frac{2m_{a}(x^{\star})}{1+m_{a}(x^{\star})}\Big]+O(\varepsilon^{2}).

Here N1​(x⋆)=|{a:x⋆⊕ea∈𝒞}|N_{1}(x^{\star})=|\{a:\ x^{\star}\oplus e_{a}\in\mathcal{C}\}| counts the codewords at Hamming distance one from the truth. If y∈𝒞y\in\mathcal{C}, the decoder returns yy, which is at distance 0, and the loss is dH​(y,x⋆)=1d_{\mathrm{H}}(y,x^{\star})=1. Otherwise dH​(y,𝒞)=1d_{\mathrm{H}}(y,\mathcal{C})=1. The codewords at distance 1 from yy are x⋆=y⊕eax^{\star}=y\oplus e_{a} and the codewords of the form y⊕eb=x⋆⊕ea⊕eby\oplus e_{b}=x^{\star}\oplus e_{a}\oplus e_{b} with b≠ab\neq a. The latter are exactly the ma​(x⋆)m_{a}(x^{\star}) words indexed by Ba​(x⋆)B_{a}(x^{\star}), and each of them is at distance 2 from x⋆x^{\star}. Uniform tie-breaking among these 1+ma​(x⋆)1+m_{a}(x^{\star}) words gives the expected loss 2​ma​(x⋆)/(1+ma​(x⋆))2m_{a}(x^{\star})/(1+m_{a}(x^{\star})). The displayed form of RMLR_{\mathrm{ML}} follows from (1). If ma​(x⋆)≤1m_{a}(x^{\star})\leq 1 for every aa, as on 2-CNF theories (see the proof of Proposition 5), the bracket equals N1​(x⋆)+#⁡{a:ma​(x⋆)=1}N_{1}(x^{\star})+\#\{a:\ m_{a}(x^{\star})=1\}. In words, each codeword at distance 1 counts 1, and each two-way tie counts 2×122\times\frac{1}{2}. ∎

Proof of Lemma 1(ii).

We show that Rgr​(ε)=ε​∑a𝔼π​Dπ​(a)+O⁡(ε2)R_{\mathrm{gr}}(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon\sum_{a}\mathbb{E}_{\pi}D_{\pi}(a)+O(\varepsilon^{2}), with the remainder bound (1), where Dπ​(a)=dH​(Gπ​(x⋆⊕ea),x⋆)D_{\pi}(a)=d_{\mathrm{H}}(G_{\pi}(x^{\star}\oplus e_{a}),x^{\star}) is the damage of one wrong answer at aa, whether this answer is accepted or not. A.2 Logical constraints

Let Φ\Phi be a satisfiable propositional formula, that is, a conjunction of clauses, over a finite set VV of atoms with |V|=n|V|=n. The code is the set 𝒞=Mod⁡(Φ)⊆{0,1}V\mathcal{C}=\operatorname{Mod}(\Phi)\subseteq\{0,1\}^{V} of models (satisfying assignments) of Φ\Phi. Every nonempty code 𝒞⊆{0,1}n\mathcal{C}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n} has this form: take for Φ\Phi the conjunction, over the words w∉𝒞w\notin\mathcal{C}, of the clause that is false exactly at ww. The truth is a model σ⋆∈𝒞\sigma^{\star}\in\mathcal{C}. For an atom xx, the true literal txt_{x} is xx if σ⋆​(x)=1\sigma^{\star}(x)=1 and ¬x\neg x otherwise; the false literal t¯x\bar{t}_{x} is the other literal on xx. The answer on xx is yx=σ⋆​(x)⊕Zxy_{x}=\sigma^{\star}(x)\oplus Z_{x}, where the ZxZ_{x} are i.i.d. Bern⁡(ε)\mathrm{Bern}(\varepsilon). The claim literal of xx is xx if yx=1y_{x}=1 and ¬x\neg x if yx=0y_{x}=0. A set LL of literals records accepted answers; requiring all its members to hold is equivalent to taking their conjunction. We write L⊧ΦmL\models_{\Phi}m if Φ∧L⊧m\Phi\wedge L\models m, that is, if every model of Φ\Phi that satisfies all literals of LL also satisfies the literal mm.

For an order π\pi of VV, the greedy decoder GπG_{\pi} (skip if implied, accept otherwise) starts with L0=∅L_{0}=\emptyset. At step tt, with x=π⁡(t)x=\pi(t), it sets Lt=Lt−1L_{t}=L_{t-1} if Lt−1⊧ΦxL_{t-1}\models_{\Phi}x or Lt−1⊧¬Φ⁡xL_{t-1}\models_{\Phi}\neg x (the atom is skipped); otherwise it sets Lt=Lt−1∪{claim literal of ​x}L_{t}=L_{t-1}\cup\{\text{claim literal of }x\} (the claim is accepted). Its output is the unique model of Φ∧Ln\Phi\wedge L_{n}. On the code Mod⁡(Φ)\operatorname{Mod}(\Phi) this is the greedy decoder of Section A.1, because “all models of Φ\Phi that satisfy LL have the same value at xx” means “L⊧ΦxL\models_{\Phi}x or L⊧¬Φ⁡xL\models_{\Phi}\neg x” whenever Φ∧L\Phi\wedge L is satisfiable. The loss is the Hamming distance, and Rgr​(ε)=𝔼Z,π​dH​(Gπ​(y),σ⋆)R_{\mathrm{gr}}(\varepsilon)=\mathbb{E}_{Z,\pi}\,d_{\mathrm{H}}(G_{\pi}(y),\sigma^{\star}) with π\pi uniform and independent of ZZ. The raw decoder outputs yy and has Rraw​(ε)=ε​nR_{\mathrm{raw}}(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon n exactly.

Lemma 16 (Well-definedness; equivalence with accept-if-consistent).

Let Φ\Phi be a satisfiable formula over VV, let π\pi be an order of VV, and let y∈{0,1}Vy\in\{0,1\}^{V} be arbitrary answers.

  1. (i)

    Φ∧Lt\Phi\wedge L_{t} is satisfiable for every tt.

  2. (ii)

    Φ∧Ln\Phi\wedge L_{n} has exactly one model, so the output Gπ​(y)G_{\pi}(y) is well defined.

  3. (iii)

    Gπ​(y)G_{\pi}(y) equals the output of the accept-if-consistent decoder. This decoder processes the atoms in the same order, starts with L0′=∅L^{\prime}_{0}=\emptyset, adds the claim literal ℓ\ell of the current atom to L′L^{\prime} if and only if Φ∧L′∧ℓ\Phi\wedge L^{\prime}\wedge\ell is satisfiable, and outputs the unique model of Φ∧Ln′\Phi\wedge L^{\prime}_{n}.

Proof.

(i) We use induction on tt. The formula Φ∧L0=Φ\Phi\wedge L_{0}=\Phi is satisfiable by assumption. A literal mm is added at step tt only if Lt−1⊧̸¬Φ⁡mL_{t-1}\not\models_{\Phi}\neg m, that is, only if Φ∧Lt−1∧m\Phi\wedge L_{t-1}\wedge m is satisfiable.

(ii) At its own step tt, each atom xx either has its value entailed by Φ∧Lt−1\Phi\wedge L_{t-1} or receives a literal in LtL_{t}. Entailment is monotone in LL, and Lt−1⊆LnL_{t-1}\subseteq L_{n}. So Φ∧Ln\Phi\wedge L_{n} entails a value for every atom. By (i) it has a model, and this model is unique because every atom’s value is entailed.

(iii) We show by induction on tt that Φ∧Lt\Phi\wedge L_{t} and Φ∧Lt′\Phi\wedge L^{\prime}_{t} have the same set of models. This holds for t=0t=0. Suppose it holds for t−1t-1; then both runs entail the same literals before step tt. Let ℓ\ell be the claim literal of the atom processed at step tt. If neither value of the atom is entailed, then ¬ℓ\neg\ell is not entailed, so ℓ\ell is consistent, and both decoders add ℓ\ell. If ℓ\ell is entailed, the greedy decoder skips the atom and the accept-if-consistent decoder adds ℓ\ell; adding an entailed literal does not change the set of models. If ¬ℓ\neg\ell is entailed, ℓ\ell is inconsistent, and both decoders leave their sets unchanged. In all cases the two sets of models remain equal. At t=nt=n this set is a single model by (ii), so the two outputs coincide. ∎

Since every nonempty code is Mod⁡(Φ)\operatorname{Mod}(\Phi) for some satisfiable Φ\Phi, Lemma 16 also shows that the greedy decoder of Section A.1 is well defined on every code.

The backbone is B={x∈V:Φ⊧tx}B=\{x\in V:\ \Phi\models t_{x}\}, the set of atoms that take the same value in every model. For a∉Ba\notin B we put

Ka={x∈V:Φ∧t¯a⊧t¯x},σ(a)=σ⋆⊕𝟏Ka,K_{a}=\{x\in V:\ \Phi\wedge\bar{t}_{a}\models\bar{t}_{x}\},\qquad\sigma^{(a)}=\sigma^{\star}\oplus\mathbf{1}_{K_{a}},

and for a∈Ba\in B we put Ka=∅K_{a}=\emptyset. When a∉Ba\notin B, the set KaK_{a} contains aa, and we call it the flip set of aa. In this case Φ∧t¯a\Phi\wedge\bar{t}_{a} is satisfiable, so it cannot entail both txt_{x} and t¯x\bar{t}_{x}, and σ(a)\sigma^{(a)} makes t¯x\bar{t}_{x} true for every x∈Kax\in K_{a}. We say that (Φ,σ⋆)(\Phi,\sigma^{\star}) has the single-flip property at aa, written (Pa), if σ(a)\sigma^{(a)} is a model of Φ\Phi. This means that flipping the forced atoms is enough to accommodate the wrong answer, without changing any other atom. Under (Pa), σ(a)\sigma^{(a)} is the unique model of Φ∧t¯a\Phi\wedge\bar{t}_{a} that agrees with σ⋆\sigma^{\star} outside KaK_{a}, because every model of Φ∧t¯a\Phi\wedge\bar{t}_{a} satisfies t¯x\bar{t}_{x} for all x∈Kax\in K_{a}. The single-error damage of the greedy decoder at aa is Dπ​(a)=dH​(Gπ​(y),σ⋆)D_{\pi}(a)=d_{\mathrm{H}}(G_{\pi}(y),\sigma^{\star}) for the answers y=σ⋆⊕eay=\sigma^{\star}\oplus e_{a}, in which only the answer on aa is wrong.

Proof of Theorem 2.

Suppose that exactly one answer is wrong, at the atom aa. Then Dπ​(a)=0D_{\pi}(a)=0 for every order π\pi when a∈Ba\in B. If a∉Ba\notin B and (Pa) holds, then for every order π\pi

Dπ​(a)=|Ka|⋅𝟏​{a​ precedes every element of ​Ka∖{a}​ in ​π},D_{\pi}(a)=|K_{a}|\cdot\mathbf{1}\{a\text{ precedes every element of }K_{a}\setminus\{a\}\text{ in }\pi\},

so that 𝔼π​Dπ​(a)=1\mathbb{E}_{\pi}D_{\pi}(a)=1 for the uniform order, and indeed for every exchangeable random order.

Case a∈Ba\in B. Here ∅⊧Φta\emptyset\models_{\Phi}t_{a}, so the atom aa is always skipped and its wrong claim t¯a\bar{t}_{a} is never accepted. All other claims are true literals. Hence all accepted literals are true, σ⋆\sigma^{\star} is a model of Φ∧Ln\Phi\wedge L_{n}, and by Lemma 16(ii) the output is σ⋆\sigma^{\star}.

Case a∉Ba\notin B under (Pa). Let τ\tau be the step at which aa is processed. For t<τt<\tau, every accepted literal is the claim of an atom with a correct answer, so LtL_{t} consists of true literals.

Step 1 (when tat_{a} is entailed). For every set SS of true literals, S⊧ΦtaS\models_{\Phi}t_{a} if and only if SS contains a literal on some atom of KaK_{a}. Indeed, S⊧ΦtaS\models_{\Phi}t_{a} if and only if Φ∧S∧t¯a\Phi\wedge S\wedge\bar{t}_{a} is unsatisfiable. If SS contains no literal on an atom of KaK_{a}, then σ(a)\sigma^{(a)} satisfies SS, because it agrees with σ⋆\sigma^{\star} outside KaK_{a}; it also satisfies t¯a\bar{t}_{a}, and it satisfies Φ\Phi by (Pa). So Φ∧S∧t¯a\Phi\wedge S\wedge\bar{t}_{a} is satisfiable, and S⊧̸ΦtaS\not\models_{\Phi}t_{a}. If SS contains txt_{x} with x∈Kax\in K_{a}, then Φ∧t¯a⊧t¯x\Phi\wedge\bar{t}_{a}\models\bar{t}_{x} contradicts txt_{x}, so Φ∧S∧t¯a\Phi\wedge S\wedge\bar{t}_{a} is unsatisfiable.

Step 2 (when the wrong claim is accepted). A literal enters LL only at the step of its own atom. So if Lτ−1L_{\tau-1} contains a literal on an atom of KaK_{a}, this atom lies in Ka∖{a}K_{a}\setminus\{a\} and precedes aa. Conversely, suppose that some x∈Ka∖{a}x\in K_{a}\setminus\{a\} is processed at a step t<τt<\tau. Either txt_{x} was added, and then Lτ−1L_{\tau-1} contains a literal on KaK_{a}; or xx was skipped. In the second case Lt−1L_{t-1} entails txt_{x} or t¯x\bar{t}_{x}; it cannot entail t¯x\bar{t}_{x}, because σ⋆\sigma^{\star} is a model of Φ∧Lt−1\Phi\wedge L_{t-1}; so Lt−1⊧ΦtxL_{t-1}\models_{\Phi}t_{x}. Then Φ∧Lt−1∧t¯a\Phi\wedge L_{t-1}\wedge\bar{t}_{a} entails both txt_{x} and t¯x\bar{t}_{x}, so it is unsatisfiable, that is, Lt−1⊧ΦtaL_{t-1}\models_{\Phi}t_{a}. By Step 1, Lt−1⊆Lτ−1L_{t-1}\subseteq L_{\tau-1} contains a literal on KaK_{a}. Together with Step 1 this shows: at step τ\tau, Lτ−1⊧ΦtaL_{\tau-1}\models_{\Phi}t_{a} if and only if some element of Ka∖{a}K_{a}\setminus\{a\} precedes aa. The wrong literal t¯a\bar{t}_{a} is never entailed at step τ\tau, because σ⋆\sigma^{\star} is a model of Φ∧Lτ−1\Phi\wedge L_{\tau-1}. Hence t¯a\bar{t}_{a} is accepted if and only if aa is the first atom of KaK_{a} in π\pi; otherwise aa is skipped.

Step 3 (rejected case). If t¯a\bar{t}_{a} is not accepted, every literal ever added is true, so the output is σ⋆\sigma^{\star} and Dπ​(a)=0D_{\pi}(a)=0.

Step 4 (accepted case). Now Ln={t¯a}∪SL_{n}=\{\bar{t}_{a}\}\cup S, where SS consists of true literals of atoms other than aa. No atom of Ka∖{a}K_{a}\setminus\{a\} contributes to SS. Indeed, such an atom xx comes after aa; at its step LL contains t¯a\bar{t}_{a}, and {t¯a}⊧Φt¯x\{\bar{t}_{a}\}\models_{\Phi}\bar{t}_{x} by the definition of KaK_{a}; so xx is skipped. Hence σ(a)\sigma^{(a)} satisfies SS (it agrees with σ⋆\sigma^{\star} outside KaK_{a}), satisfies t¯a\bar{t}_{a}, and satisfies Φ\Phi by (Pa). By Lemma 16(ii) the output is σ(a)\sigma^{(a)}, and Dπ​(a)=|Ka|D_{\pi}(a)=|K_{a}|.

Expectation. For the uniform order, and for every exchangeable random order, each of the |Ka||K_{a}| atoms of KaK_{a} is equally likely to come first among them. So aa comes first with probability 1/|Ka|1/|K_{a}|, and 𝔼π​Dπ​(a)=|Ka|⋅|Ka|−1=1\mathbb{E}_{\pi}D_{\pi}(a)=|K_{a}|\cdot|K_{a}|^{-1}=1. ∎

Proof of Proposition 3.

We show that if every clause of Φ\Phi has at most two literals, then (Pa) holds for every truth σ⋆∈𝒞\sigma^{\star}\in\mathcal{C} and every atom a∉Ba\notin B. Let EE be the set of literals entailed by Φ∧t¯a\Phi\wedge\bar{t}_{a}. Since Φ∧t¯a\Phi\wedge\bar{t}_{a} is satisfiable, EE contains no complementary pair. By definition, for x∈Kax\in K_{a} the literal t¯x\bar{t}_{x} lies in EE, and σ(a)\sigma^{(a)} makes it true. Take a clause p∨qp\vee q of Φ\Phi and suppose that σ(a)\sigma^{(a)} falsifies both pp and qq. If neither atom lies in KaK_{a}, then σ(a)\sigma^{(a)} agrees with σ⋆\sigma^{\star} on both atoms, and σ⋆\sigma^{\star} satisfies the clause; this is a contradiction. So we may assume that atom⁡(p)∈Ka\operatorname{atom}(p)\in K_{a}, where atom⁡(p)\operatorname{atom}(p) denotes the atom of the literal pp. Then ¬p\neg p is true under σ(a)\sigma^{(a)}, and it equals t¯atom⁡(p)\bar{t}_{\operatorname{atom}(p)}, which lies in EE. From Φ⊧p∨q\Phi\models p\vee q we get q∈Eq\in E. If atom⁡(q)∈Ka\operatorname{atom}(q)\in K_{a}, the unique literal of EE on this atom is t¯atom⁡(q)\bar{t}_{\operatorname{atom}(q)}, which σ(a)\sigma^{(a)} makes true; so qq is true, a contradiction. If atom⁡(q)∉Ka\operatorname{atom}(q)\notin K_{a}, then t¯atom⁡(q)∉E\bar{t}_{\operatorname{atom}(q)}\notin E, so q=tatom⁡(q)q=t_{\operatorname{atom}(q)}; this literal is true under σ⋆\sigma^{\star} and hence under σ(a)\sigma^{(a)}, again a contradiction. Finally, take a unit clause (p)(p). Then p∈Ep\in E, and p=tatom⁡(p)p=t_{\operatorname{atom}(p)} because σ⋆⊧p\sigma^{\star}\models p. If atom⁡(p)\operatorname{atom}(p) were in KaK_{a}, then EE would contain both pp and t¯atom⁡(p)=¬p\bar{t}_{\operatorname{atom}(p)}=\neg p; so atom⁡(p)∉Ka\operatorname{atom}(p)\notin K_{a}, and σ(a)\sigma^{(a)} satisfies pp. ∎

Implication theories.

For a directed graph G=(V,A)G=(V,A) let ΦG=⋀(u,v)∈A(¬u∨v)\Phi_{G}=\bigwedge_{(u,v)\in A}(\neg u\vee v). Identify an assignment with its set of true atoms. The models of ΦG\Phi_{G} are then the closed sets: the sets MM such that u∈Mu\in M and (u,v)∈A(u,v)\in A imply v∈Mv\in M (the up-closed sets of the preorder generated by GG). For X⊆VX\subseteq V, let cl⁡(X)\operatorname{cl}(X) be the smallest closed set that contains XX. Since ∅\emptyset and VV are models, the backbone is empty. Let M⋆M^{\star} be the true set, let reach⁡(a)\operatorname{reach}(a) be the set of vertices reachable from aa (including aa), and let anc⁡(a)\operatorname{anc}(a) be the set of vertices from which aa is reachable (including aa). Then:

  • •

    for a false positive (a∉M⋆a\notin M^{\star}), Ka=reach⁡(a)∖M⋆K_{a}=\operatorname{reach}(a)\setminus M^{\star} and σ(a)=M⋆∪reach⁡(a)\sigma^{(a)}=M^{\star}\cup\operatorname{reach}(a); hence |Ka|=ca:=|cl⁡(M⋆∪{a})∖M⋆||K_{a}|=c_{a}:=|\operatorname{cl}(M^{\star}\cup\{a\})\setminus M^{\star}|, the cone of aa;

  • •

    for a false negative (a∈M⋆a\in M^{\star}), Ka=anc⁡(a)∩M⋆K_{a}=\operatorname{anc}(a)\cap M^{\star} and σ(a)=M⋆∖anc⁡(a)\sigma^{(a)}=M^{\star}\setminus\operatorname{anc}(a).

Indeed, the models of ΦG∧a\Phi_{G}\wedge a are the closed sets that contain reach⁡(a)\operatorname{reach}(a); the smallest is reach⁡(a)\operatorname{reach}(a) and the largest is VV. So the literals entailed by ΦG∧a\Phi_{G}\wedge a are exactly the positive literals on reach⁡(a)\operatorname{reach}(a). For a∉M⋆a\notin M^{\star} we have t¯a=a\bar{t}_{a}=a, and t¯x\bar{t}_{x} is the positive literal xx exactly when x∉M⋆x\notin M^{\star}; this gives Ka=reach⁡(a)∖M⋆K_{a}=\operatorname{reach}(a)\setminus M^{\star}. Since M⋆M^{\star} is closed, M⋆∪reach⁡(a)M^{\star}\cup\operatorname{reach}(a) is closed and equals cl⁡(M⋆∪{a})\operatorname{cl}(M^{\star}\cup\{a\}). Dually, the models of ΦG∧¬a\Phi_{G}\wedge\neg a are the closed sets contained in V∖anc⁡(a)V\setminus\operatorname{anc}(a), which is itself closed; the smallest is ∅\emptyset and the largest is V∖anc⁡(a)V\setminus\operatorname{anc}(a). So the literals entailed by ΦG∧¬a\Phi_{G}\wedge\neg a are exactly the negative literals on anc⁡(a)\operatorname{anc}(a). For a∈M⋆a\in M^{\star} we have t¯a=¬a\bar{t}_{a}=\neg a, and t¯x=¬x\bar{t}_{x}=\neg x exactly when x∈M⋆x\in M^{\star}; this gives Ka=anc⁡(a)∩M⋆K_{a}=\operatorname{anc}(a)\cap M^{\star}.

Remark 17 (The random order is essential).

For a fixed order the single-error damage takes only the values 00 and |Ka||K_{a}|. Under a random order, the wrong claim is accepted with probability 1/|Ka|1/|K_{a}|, and then it damages exactly |Ka||K_{a}| atoms. A fixed order can make every error of one type maximally damaging. Consider the chain v1→v2→…→vnv_{1}\to v_{2}\to\dots\to v_{n} (clauses ¬vi∨vi+1\neg v_{i}\vee v_{i+1}), whose models are the up-sets {vj,…,vn}\{v_{j},\dots,v_{n}\} and ∅\emptyset. For a false positive at aa, the flip set Ka=reach⁡(a)∖M⋆K_{a}=\operatorname{reach}(a)\setminus M^{\star} consists of aa and the false atoms after it on the chain, and the wrong claim is accepted if and only if aa is asked before every other atom of KaK_{a}. So the topological order v1,v2,…,vnv_{1},v_{2},\dots,v_{n} accepts every false positive and lets it corrupt every false atom reachable from it, while the reverse order vn,…,v1v_{n},\dots,v_{1} rejects every false positive with |Ka|≥2|K_{a}|\geq 2. For example, with the chain a→ba\to b, the truth “both false” and the wrong answer a=1a=1, the order (a,b)(a,b) accepts aa, then finds bb implied true, and has damage 2; the order (b,a)(b,a) accepts b=0b=0, then finds aa implied false, and has damage 0. For false negatives the roles of the two orders are exchanged: Ka=anc⁡(a)∩M⋆K_{a}=\operatorname{anc}(a)\cap M^{\star} consists of aa and the true atoms before it, and the reverse topological order is the damaging one.

Horn hubs.

For integers k≥1k\geq 1 and s≥2s\geq 2, the Horn hub Hk,sH_{k,s} has the atom aa and, for each i=1,…,ki=1,\dots,k, the atoms bi,1,…,bi,s−1,cib_{i,1},\dots,b_{i,s-1},c_{i}; so n=1+k​sn=1+ks. Its rules are bi,1∧⋯∧bi,s−1∧a→cib_{i,1}\wedge\dots\wedge b_{i,s-1}\wedge a\to c_{i} for i=1,…,ki=1,\dots,k, each with a body of ss atoms. Satisfiability criterion. Let L′L^{\prime} be a set of literals without complementary pairs. We claim that Φ∧L′\Phi\wedge L^{\prime} is unsatisfiable if and only if a∈L′a\in L^{\prime} and Ti⊆L′T_{i}\subseteq L^{\prime} for some ii, that is, L′L^{\prime} falsifies every literal of some clause CiC_{i} other than ¬a\neg a. The run with the wrong claim aa. All other claims are the true literals, the members of the sets TiT_{i}. Let τ\tau be the step of aa.

Remark 18 (Where the single-flip property fails).

In Hk,sH_{k,s} the formula Φ∧a\Phi\wedge a entails nothing new. Indeed, by the satisfiability criterion {a,ℓ}\{a,\ell\} is consistent for every literal ℓ\ell on another atom, because each TiT_{i} has s≥2s\geq 2 literals. So Ka={a}K_{a}=\{a\} and σ(a)=M⋆∪{a}\sigma^{(a)}=M^{\star}\cup\{a\}, which violates every clause CiC_{i} and is not a model. The wrong literal alone does not imply additional incorrect values. These values are implied later, when the wrong literal is combined with correct literals. Acceptance is determined by the ss-element blocks rather than by the flip set. The single-flip property can also fail for false negatives. Change the signs of the literals on aa and on cic_{i} in every clause; this gives the rules bi,1∧⋯∧bi,s−1∧ci→ab_{i,1}\wedge\dots\wedge b_{i,s-1}\wedge c_{i}\to a (for s=2s=2, the rules bi∧ci→ab_{i}\wedge c_{i}\to a). Take the truth in which all atoms are true, and a false negative on aa. The unsatisfiability criterion becomes: ¬a∈L′\neg a\in L^{\prime} and some block has all its true literals in L′L^{\prime}. The proof above, with the literals of each block exchanged, gives the same damage law. For comparison with ML, when k≥2k\geq 2 the word M⋆∪{a}M^{\star}\cup\{a\} has M⋆M^{\star} as its unique nearest codeword, because flipping a single atom of a block repairs only one of the kk violated clauses. So the ML single-error damage at aa is 0.

General Horn theories.

A definite Horn theory is a conjunction of rules b1∧⋯∧br→hb_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge b_{r}\to h over atoms, where {b1,…,br}\{b_{1},\dots,b_{r}\} is the body and hh the head of the rule. Identify a model with its set of true atoms. The models are then the closed sets, that is, the sets that contain the head of every rule whose body they contain. For X⊆VX\subseteq V, cl⁡(X)\operatorname{cl}(X) is the smallest closed set that contains XX, obtained by repeatedly adding conclusions whose premises are already present. For a closed truth M⋆M^{\star} and an atom a∉M⋆a\notin M^{\star}, the cone of aa is ca=|cl⁡(M⋆∪{a})∖M⋆|c_{a}=|\operatorname{cl}(M^{\star}\cup\{a\})\setminus M^{\star}|; this extends the cone of implication theories.

Conjecture 19 (Body-size law).

For every s≥2s\geq 2 there is a constant Cs<∞C_{s}<\infty with the following property. Let Φ\Phi be a definite Horn theory whose rule bodies have at most ss atoms, let M⋆M^{\star} be a closed set, and let a∉M⋆a\notin M^{\star}. Then a single false positive at aa (all other answers correct) has, for uniform π\pi,

𝔼π​Dπ​(a)≤Cs​ca 1−1/s.\mathbb{E}_{\pi}D_{\pi}(a)\ \leq\ C_{s}\,c_{a}^{\,1-1/s}.

By Theorem 6 the exponent cannot be lowered: the hub Hk,sH_{k,s} has ca=k+1c_{a}=k+1 and 𝔼π​Dπ​(a)∼Γ⁡(1+1s)​k1−1/s\mathbb{E}_{\pi}D_{\pi}(a)\sim\Gamma(1+\frac{1}{s})\,k^{1-1/s}. For s=1s=1, that is, for implication theories, the statement holds with C1=1C_{1}=1 and with equality: there |Ka|=ca|K_{a}|=c_{a} for a false positive, and 𝔼π​Dπ​(a)=1\mathbb{E}_{\pi}D_{\pi}(a)=1 by Theorems 2 and 3. A corresponding bound for false negatives remains open; it requires a way to measure the atoms affected when a true premise is removed. In the simulations of Section B, which also test Conjecture 19, false-negative damages reach 1.481.48.

A.3 Entity resolution

The items are [m]={1,…,m}[m]=\{1,\dots,m\}. The code is the set of partitions of [m][m], written as vectors of (m2)\binom{m}{2} pair indicators xu​v=𝟏{u∼v}x_{uv}=\mathbf{1}\{u\sim v\}, where u∼vu\sim v means that uu and vv lie in the same block. The constraints are transitivity, xu​v∧xv​w→xu​wx_{uv}\wedge x_{vw}\to x_{uw}. Each pair ee carries an independent answer ye=xe⋆⊕ξey_{e}=x^{\star}_{e}\oplus\xi_{e} with ξe∼Bern⁡(δ)\xi_{e}\sim\mathrm{Bern}(\delta). In this section the true partition x⋆x^{\star} has a single cluster, so every flip is a false “different”, and δ\delta is the false-split rate. The loss LL is the number of pairs on which the output partition disagrees with the truth; here it is the number of pairs that the output separates.

The pipeline UπU_{\pi} is the transitivity pruning of Wang et al. (2013). It maintains a partition of [m][m] into blocks and a set of ≠\neq constraints between blocks. It processes the pairs in the order π\pi. For a pair e={u,v}e=\{u,v\}, it skips ee if uu and vv lie in the same block or if their blocks carry a ≠\neq constraint. Otherwise it queries the answer yey_{e}. On “same” it merges the two blocks, and the merged block inherits all ≠\neq constraints of both; on “different” it adds a ≠\neq constraint between the two blocks. Its output is the final partition into blocks.

For an order π\pi of the pairs, TπT_{\pi} is the spanning tree obtained by scanning π\pi and keeping a pair if and only if it joins two different components of the pairs kept so far. This is Kruskal’s algorithm (Kruskal, 1956) for the edge weights “position in π\pi”, so TπT_{\pi} is the minimum spanning tree for these weights. It depends on π\pi only, not on the answers. With all answers correct, its edges are exactly the queried pairs; we therefore use it as a reference tree even in noisy runs. For a spanning tree TT of the complete graph KmK_{m}, dT​(u,v)d_{T}(u,v) is the number of edges on the path from uu to vv in TT. For an edge e∈Te\in T, nen_{e} and m−nem-n_{e} are the numbers of vertices of the two components of T−eT-e. The Wiener index of TT is

W⁡(T)=∑{u,v}dT​(u,v)=∑e∈Tne​(m−ne),W(T)=\sum_{\{u,v\}}d_{T}(u,v)=\sum_{e\in T}n_{e}(m-n_{e}),

where the second form counts, for each edge ee, the ne​(m−ne)n_{e}(m-n_{e}) pairs whose path uses ee. We also write W2​(T)=∑{u,v}dT​(u,v)2W_{2}(T)=\sum_{\{u,v\}}d_{T}(u,v)^{2}.

Lemma 20 (Union-find is the greedy decoder).

For every order π\pi of the pairs and all answers, the union-find pipeline UπU_{\pi} equals the greedy decoder on the partition code. That is, it skips exactly the pairs whose relation is entailed by the answers accepted so far, it accepts the answer on every other pair, and its output is the unique partition that satisfies all accepted answers.

Proof.

Let LL be a set of accepted literals, each an equality u∼vu\sim v or an inequality u≁vu\not\sim v, and assume that LL is satisfiable, that is, that some partition satisfies all of them. Call the connected components of the graph of accepted equalities the equality-components. We claim: (a) LL entails u∼vu\sim v if and only if uu and vv lie in the same equality-component; (b) LL entails u≁vu\not\sim v if and only if some accepted inequality joins the equality-component of uu to that of vv.

(a) If uu and vv are joined by a path of accepted equalities, transitivity gives u∼vu\sim v in every model. Conversely, consider the partition into equality-components. It satisfies every accepted equality. It also satisfies every accepted inequality: in any model every equality-component lies in one block, so a satisfiable LL contains no inequality inside an equality-component. This partition separates any two points of different equality-components, so for such points LL does not entail u∼vu\sim v.

(b) If an accepted inequality joins a point xx of the component of uu to a point yy of the component of vv, then every model has u∼xu\sim x, x≁yx\not\sim y and y∼vy\sim v, hence u≁vu\not\sim v by transitivity. Conversely, suppose that no accepted inequality joins the two components. If the two components coincide, LL entails u∼vu\sim v and, being satisfiable, does not entail u≁vu\not\sim v. Otherwise, merge these two components and keep all other equality-components as blocks. The resulting partition satisfies every accepted equality and every accepted inequality, and in it u∼vu\sim v; so LL does not entail u≁vu\not\sim v.

We now compare the two decoders step by step. Suppose that before some step both have accepted the same satisfiable set LL; this holds at the start, with L=∅L=\emptyset. The blocks of the pipeline are the equality-components of LL, because a merge happens exactly when an equality is accepted. Two blocks carry a ≠\neq constraint if and only if an accepted inequality joins them, because constraints are created by accepted inequalities and inherited through merges. By (a) and (b), the pipeline skips the current pair exactly when LL entails its relation, which is the rule of the greedy decoder; otherwise both decoders accept the answer. An accepted answer is consistent with LL, because its negation is not entailed, so the new set is again satisfiable. By induction, the two decoders accept the same literals at every step. At the end, the final blocks form the partition into equality-components, which satisfies LnL_{n} by the proof of (a); by Lemma 16(ii) it is the unique model of LnL_{n}, that is, the output of the greedy decoder. ∎

The full flip vector ξ\xi assigns a potential error to every pair, but the pipeline reads ξe\xi_{e} only when it queries that pair. The decision to query ee uses only earlier answers, so its unobserved error is still independent of that decision. This gives the same distribution as independently flipping each queried answer.

Proof of Lemma 7.

Let the truth be one cluster, and fix an order π\pi and a flip vector ξ\xi. Let F={e∈Tπ:ξe=1}F=\{e\in T_{\pi}:\ \xi_{e}=1\} be the set of flipped tree edges. For a pair {u,v}\{u,v\}, let k⁡(u,v)k(u,v) be the number of edges of FF on the path from uu to vv in TπT_{\pi}. We show that k⁡(u,v)=0k(u,v)=0 implies that uu and vv end in the same block, and that k⁡(u,v)=1k(u,v)=1 implies that they end in different blocks. Consequently N1≤Lπ≤N≥1N_{1}\leq L_{\pi}\leq N_{\geq 1}, where NjN_{j} (respectively N≥jN_{\geq j}) is the number of pairs with k⁡(u,v)=jk(u,v)=j (respectively k⁡(u,v)≥jk(u,v)\geq j).

Let κt\kappa_{t} be the partition of [m][m] into the components of the edges of TπT_{\pi} among the first tt pairs of π\pi. It equals the partition into the components of all of the first tt pairs, because Kruskal’s algorithm keeps a pair exactly when it joins two components. Let PtP_{t} be the partition of the pipeline into blocks after tt pairs.

(A) PtP_{t} refines κt\kappa_{t}: every pipeline block lies inside one κt\kappa_{t}-component. We use induction on tt; blocks change only by merges. A merge at step tt happens on a queried pair e={u,v}e=\{u,v\}. After step tt, uu and vv lie in the same κt\kappa_{t}-component: either ee joins two κt−1\kappa_{t-1}-components, and then e∈Tπe\in T_{\pi}, or uu and vv were already in one component. The merged block is the union of two blocks, each contained in a κt−1\kappa_{t-1}-component by the induction hypothesis, and both of these components lie inside the κt\kappa_{t}-component of uu.

(B) At every time tt, every ≠\neq constraint joins two blocks that lie in the same κt\kappa_{t}-component. A constraint is created at some step on a queried pair {u,v}\{u,v\}, and from then on it joins the current block of uu and the current block of vv, because constraints are inherited through merges. As in (A), uu and vv lie in one κ\kappa-component from that step on, since the partitions κt\kappa_{t} only become coarser. By (A), the current blocks of uu and vv lie inside this component.

(C) Every edge e={u,v}∈Tπe=\{u,v\}\in T_{\pi} is queried. At its step tt, the points uu and vv lie in different κt−1\kappa_{t-1}-components, by the definition of TπT_{\pi}. By (A) they lie in different blocks. By (B) no ≠\neq constraint joins these two blocks. So ee is queried. Since the truth is one cluster, the query merges the two blocks if ξe=0\xi_{e}=0, and it creates a ≠\neq constraint between them if ξe=1\xi_{e}=1.

Blocks never split. By (C), the two ends of every edge of Tπ∖FT_{\pi}\setminus F end in the same block. So every component of Tπ∖FT_{\pi}\setminus F (a fragment) lies inside one final block. This is the first claim, because k⁡(u,v)=0k(u,v)=0 means that uu and vv lie in the same fragment. For the second claim, let f={x,y}f=\{x,y\} be the unique flipped edge on the path from uu to vv, with uu on the side of xx. By (C), at the step of ff a ≠\neq constraint is placed between the block of xx and the block of yy. Two blocks joined by a ≠\neq constraint are never merged, because a merge follows only a query, and a query is made only between unconstrained blocks. The constraint is inherited by every later block that contains xx or yy. So xx and yy end in different blocks. The paths from uu to xx and from yy to vv contain no flipped edge, so by the first claim uu ends with xx and vv ends with yy. Hence uu and vv end in different blocks. Since the loss counts the separated pairs, the pairs with k=1k=1 are counted and the pairs with k=0k=0 are not, which gives N1≤Lπ≤N≥1N_{1}\leq L_{\pi}\leq N_{\geq 1}. ∎

Proof of Theorem 8.

We show that for every order π\pi and every δ∈[0,1]\delta\in[0,1], with d=dTπ​(u,v)d=d_{T_{\pi}}(u,v) in each summand,

δ​W​(Tπ)−δ2​W2​(Tπ)≤∑{u,v}d​δ​(1−δ)d−1≤𝔼ξ​Lπ≤∑{u,v}(1−(1−δ)d)≤δ​W​(Tπ).\delta\,W(T_{\pi})-\delta^{2}W_{2}(T_{\pi})\ \leq\ \sum_{\{u,v\}}d\,\delta(1-\delta)^{d-1}\ \leq\ \mathbb{E}_{\xi}L_{\pi}\ \leq\ \sum_{\{u,v\}}\big(1-(1-\delta)^{d}\big)\ \leq\ \delta\,W(T_{\pi}).

Take expectations over ξ\xi in Lemma 7. The tree TπT_{\pi} does not depend on ξ\xi, so the flips on the dd edges of the path from uu to vv are i.i.d. Bern⁡(δ)\mathrm{Bern}(\delta), and k⁡(u,v)k(u,v) is binomial with parameters dd and δ\delta. Hence ℙ⁡(k⁡(u,v)=1)=d​δ​(1−δ)d−1\mathbb{P}(k(u,v)=1)=d\delta(1-\delta)^{d-1} and ℙ⁡(k⁡(u,v)≥1)=1−(1−δ)d\mathbb{P}(k(u,v)\geq 1)=1-(1-\delta)^{d}, which gives the two middle inequalities. For the outer ones, d​δ​(1−δ)d−1≥d​δ​(1−(d−1)​δ)≥d​δ−d2​δ2d\delta(1-\delta)^{d-1}\geq d\delta(1-(d-1)\delta)\geq d\delta-d^{2}\delta^{2} by Bernoulli’s inequality, and 1−(1−δ)d≤d​δ1-(1-\delta)^{d}\leq d\delta. Summing over pairs gives the bounds, and W2​(Tπ)≤(m2)​(m−1)2W_{2}(T_{\pi})\leq\binom{m}{2}(m-1)^{2} because d≤m−1d\leq m-1. With exactly one flip, on the pair ee, we have k⁡(u,v)∈{0,1}k(u,v)\in\{0,1\} for all pairs. If e∈Tπe\in T_{\pi}, then Lπ=N1L_{\pi}=N_{1} is the number of pairs whose tree path uses ee, that is, ne​(m−ne)n_{e}(m-n_{e}). If e∉Tπe\notin T_{\pi}, then F=∅F=\emptyset and Lπ=0L_{\pi}=0; indeed, the pair ee is never queried when all earlier answers are correct. ∎

With no wrong answer, the pipeline makes exactly m−1m-1 queries, namely the edges of TπT_{\pi}. By (C) in the proof of Lemma 7 every tree edge is queried. A pair outside the tree arrives when its two ends already lie in one κ\kappa-component; with all answers correct, every tree edge so far has merged its blocks, so the blocks coincide with the κ\kappa-components and the pair is skipped.

Known results on the random minimum spanning tree.

For uniform π\pi, the tree TπT_{\pi} is distributed as the minimum spanning tree MSTm\mathrm{MST}_{m} of KmK_{m} with i.i.d. continuous edge weights. We use two known results on MSTm\mathrm{MST}_{m}.

  • (F1)

    (Addario-Berry et al., 2009) 𝔼​diam⁡(MSTm)=Θ⁡(m1/3)\mathbb{E}\operatorname{diam}(\mathrm{MST}_{m})=\Theta(m^{1/3}), where diam\operatorname{diam} is the largest tree distance between two vertices.

  • (F2)

    (Addario-Berry et al., 2017, Theorem 1.1) The tree MSTm\mathrm{MST}_{m}, with distances multiplied by m−1/3m^{-1/3} and with the uniform probability measure on its vertices, converges in distribution, in the Gromov–Hausdorff–Prokhorov topology, to a random compact measured real tree (ℳ,d,μ)(\mathcal{M},d,\mu). Let DmD_{m} be the tree distance between two independent uniform vertices of MSTm\mathrm{MST}_{m}. By the standard Gromov–Prokhorov consequence of this convergence, Dm/m1/3D_{m}/m^{1/3} converges in distribution to D:=d⁡(ζ1,ζ2)D:=d(\zeta_{1},\zeta_{2}), where, given (ℳ,d,μ)(\mathcal{M},d,\mu), the points ζ1\zeta_{1} and ζ2\zeta_{2} are independent with law μ\mu. Broutin and Marckert (2023, Theorem 1.1 and Proposition 6.5) identify the same measured limit and show that, for a point ζ\zeta sampled from μ\mu, almost surely μ⁡(B⁡(ζ,r))≤r5/2\mu(B(\zeta,r))\leq r^{5/2} for all sufficiently small r>0r>0. Thus μ⁡({ζ})=0\mu(\{\zeta\})=0 almost surely. Conditional independence then gives ℙ⁡(D=0)=𝔼⁡[μ⁡({ζ1})]=0\mathbb{P}(D=0)=\mathbb{E}[\mu(\{\zeta_{1}\})]=0, so ℙ⁡(D>0)=1\mathbb{P}(D>0)=1.

The scale m−1/3m^{-1/3} also appears in this tree’s edge-weight-resampling noise threshold (Israeli and Peled, 2024).

For a fixed query order, the loss need not increase when additional answers are flipped.
