So the Bayes risk is at least 12​δ​(1−δ)m−2​∑e∈Tne​(m−ne)=12​δ​(1−δ)m−2​W​(T)\frac{1}{2}\delta(1-\delta)^{m-2}\sum_{e\in T}n_{e}(m-n_{e})=\frac{1}{2}\delta(1-\delta)^{m-2}W(T). The maximum risk is at least the Bayes risk, and (i) gives the second inequality. Part (ii) assumes that the observed tree is fixed in advance. The pipeline UπU_{\pi} can change its queries in response to answers, even though its noiseless query set is TπT_{\pi}, so the bound does not directly apply to it. ∎

Similarity order.

The items carry embeddings X1,…,XmX_{1},\dots,X_{m}, i.i.d. with a density ff on [0,1]d[0,1]^{d} that is bounded below by f0>0f_{0}>0. The pairs are processed in increasing order of the Euclidean distance |Xu−Xv||X_{u}-X_{v}| (most similar first), as in the order by decreasing match probability of Wang et al. (2013). Then TπT_{\pi} is the Euclidean minimum spanning tree EMSTm\mathrm{EMST}_{m} of the points, which is almost surely unique. The order is independent of the answers, so Theorem 8 gives the first-order risk δ​W​(EMSTm)\delta\,W(\mathrm{EMST}_{m}) conditionally on the embeddings. Throughout, log\log is the natural logarithm.

Proof of Theorem 11.

Let μf=𝔼​|X1−X2|>0\mu_{f}=\mathbb{E}|X_{1}-X_{2}|>0. We show that for every m≥2m\geq 2 with f0​m≥2​log⁡mf_{0}m\geq 2\log m,

𝔼​W​(EMSTm)(m2)≥μf−d/m4​d​(f0​m2​log⁡m)1/d=cd,f​(mlog⁡m)1/d​(1−o⁡(1)),cd,f=μf4​d​(f02)1/d,\frac{\mathbb{E}\,W(\mathrm{EMST}_{m})}{\binom{m}{2}}\ \geq\ \frac{\mu_{f}-\sqrt{d}/m}{4\sqrt{d}}\Big(\frac{f_{0}\,m}{2\log m}\Big)^{1/d}=c_{d,f}\Big(\frac{m}{\log m}\Big)^{1/d}\big(1-o(1)\big),\qquad c_{d,f}=\frac{\mu_{f}}{4\sqrt{d}}\Big(\frac{f_{0}}{2}\Big)^{1/d},

and that for d=1d=1 and any continuous distribution W⁡(EMSTm)/(m2)=(m+1)/3W(\mathrm{EMST}_{m})/\binom{m}{2}=(m+1)/3 exactly.

The proof bounds the length of the longest tree edge, then uses it to show that paths between distant points must contain many edges.

(1) Bottleneck property. For r>0r>0 let G⁡(X,r)G(X;r) be the geometric graph on the points with an edge between any two points at distance at most rr. The longest edge ℓmax\ell_{\max} of EMSTm\mathrm{EMST}_{m} is at most any rr for which G⁡(X,r)G(X;r) is connected. Indeed, suppose that G⁡(X,r)G(X;r) is connected and that an edge ee of EMSTm\mathrm{EMST}_{m} is longer than rr. Removing ee splits the points into two sides. Some edge of G⁡(X,r)G(X;r) crosses this cut, and exchanging it for ee gives a lighter spanning tree, which is a contradiction.

(2) Tiling. Let x=(f0​m/(2​log⁡m))1/dx=(f_{0}m/(2\log m))^{1/d}, which is at least 1 by assumption, and let N=⌊x⌋≥x/2N=\lfloor x\rfloor\geq x/2. Tile [0,1]d[0,1]^{d} by NdN^{d} cubes of side 1/N1/N. Each cube receives a given point with probability at least f0​N−d≥f0​x−d=2​log⁡m/mf_{0}N^{-d}\geq f_{0}x^{-d}=2\log m/m. So the probability that some cube is empty is at most Nd​(1−2​log⁡m/m)m≤xd​m−2=f0/(2​m​log⁡m)≤1/mN^{d}(1-2\log m/m)^{m}\leq x^{d}m^{-2}=f_{0}/(2m\log m)\leq 1/m; the last step uses f0≤1≤2​log⁡mf_{0}\leq 1\leq 2\log m, where f0≤1f_{0}\leq 1 because ff integrates to 1 on the unit cube. Suppose that no cube is empty. Two points in the same cube are within distance d/N\sqrt{d}/N, and two points in face-adjacent cubes are within distance d+3/N≤2​d/N\sqrt{d+3}/N\leq 2\sqrt{d}/N. The face-adjacency graph of the cubes is connected, and every point lies in a cube. So G⁡(X,2​d/N)G(X;2\sqrt{d}/N) is connected, and by (1), ℓmax≤2​d/N≤4​d/x\ell_{\max}\leq 2\sqrt{d}/N\leq 4\sqrt{d}/x. Call this event AA; we have shown ℙ⁡(Ac)≤1/m\mathbb{P}(A^{c})\leq 1/m.

(3) Paths are long. On AA, the tree path from uu to vv consists of dT​(u,v)d_{T}(u,v) edges of length at most ℓmax\ell_{\max}, and it covers the Euclidean distance |Xu−Xv||X_{u}-X_{v}|. So dT​(u,v)≥|Xu−Xv|/ℓmax≥x​|Xu−Xv|/(4​d)d_{T}(u,v)\geq|X_{u}-X_{v}|/\ell_{\max}\geq x|X_{u}-X_{v}|/(4\sqrt{d}), where T=EMSTmT=\mathrm{EMST}_{m}. Hence

𝔼​W​(EMSTm)≥x4​d​𝔼​[𝟏A​∑{u,v}|Xu−Xv|]≥x4​d​(m2)​(μf−dm),\mathbb{E}\,W(\mathrm{EMST}_{m})\ \geq\ \frac{x}{4\sqrt{d}}\,\mathbb{E}\Big[\mathbf{1}_{A}\sum_{\{u,v\}}|X_{u}-X_{v}|\Big]\ \geq\ \frac{x}{4\sqrt{d}}\binom{m}{2}\Big(\mu_{f}-\frac{\sqrt{d}}{m}\Big),

because |Xu−Xv|≤d|X_{u}-X_{v}|\leq\sqrt{d} and ℙ⁡(Ac)≤1/m\mathbb{P}(A^{c})\leq 1/m. Dividing by (m2)\binom{m}{2} gives the bound.

(4) The case d=1d=1. For distinct points on a line, which occur almost surely under a continuous distribution, the minimum spanning tree is the path through the points in sorted order. The path PmP_{m} has W⁡(Pm)=∑i=1m−1i⁡(m−i)=(m+13)W(P_{m})=\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}i(m-i)=\binom{m+1}{3}, so W⁡(Pm)/(m2)=(m+1)/3W(P_{m})/\binom{m}{2}=(m+1)/3.

Relative to Proposition 10, the similarity-first amplification is larger by order m2/3m^{2/3} in d=1d=1 and at least order m1/6/log⁡mm^{1/6}/\sqrt{\log m} in d=2d=2. Thus, under these embedding assumptions and for all sufficiently large mm, similarity ordering within a cluster has higher first-order risk than random ordering and pivot ordering. ∎

For d=2d=2, sharper amplification exponents would require finer control of planar MST path geometry; existing planar scaling results give bounds on path dimension (Aizenman et al., 1999). For d≥3d\geq 3 the bound (m/log⁡m)1/d(m/\log m)^{1/d} is below m1/3m^{1/3} and gives no comparison with random order.

Several clusters.

There are KK latent clusters C1,…,CKC_{1},\dots,C_{K} of sizes s1,…,sKs_{1},\dots,s_{K}, and n=∑isin=\sum_{i}s_{i} items. All (n2)\binom{n}{2} pairs are processed in a uniformly random order π\pi by the union-find pipeline UπU_{\pi} of Section A.3. A pair inside a cluster is a within pair, and a pair between two clusters is a cross pair. The answer on a within pair is flipped to a false “different” with probability εw\varepsilon_{w}, and the answer on a cross pair is flipped to a false “same” with probability εx\varepsilon_{x}; all flips are independent. The loss is the number of false-positive (FP) pairs, which the output wrongly puts together, plus the number of false-negative (FN) pairs, which the output wrongly separates. We generate the uniform order by attaching independent Unif⁡[0,1]\mathrm{Unif}[0,1] arrival times to the pairs. For N≥1N\geq 1 and p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1], G⁡(N,p)G(N,p) is the Erdős–Rényi random graph on NN vertices, in which each pair of vertices is an edge independently with probability pp. As in Section A.3, MSTs\mathrm{MST}_{s} is the minimum spanning tree of KsK_{s} with i.i.d. continuous edge weights, and WW is the Wiener index.

For sizes sAs_{A} and sBs_{B}, consider only two clusters AA and BB, with all pairs of A∪BA\cup B in uniformly random order. All answers are correct except one cross pair e={u,v}e=\{u,v\}, with u∈Au\in A and v∈Bv\in B, which is answered “same”. Let DeD_{e} be the loss, and let g⁡(sA,sB)=𝔼π​Deg(s_{A},s_{B})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}D_{e}; by symmetry it does not depend on the choice of ee. We split g=gFP+gFNg=g_{\mathrm{FP}}+g_{\mathrm{FN}} into the expected numbers of FP and FN pairs, and we write g⁡(s)=g⁡(s,s)g(s)=g(s,s).

Proof of Theorem 12.

We show that, with ε=max⁡(εw,εx)\varepsilon=\max(\varepsilon_{w},\varepsilon_{x}) and N=(n2)N=\binom{n}{2},

RU​(εw,εx)=εw​∑i=1K𝔼​W​(MSTsi)+εx​∑i<jsi​sj​g​(si,sj)+O⁡(ε2),R_{U}(\varepsilon_{w},\varepsilon_{x})=\varepsilon_{w}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\,W(\mathrm{MST}_{s_{i}})+\varepsilon_{x}\sum_{i<j}s_{i}s_{j}\,g(s_{i},s_{j})+O(\varepsilon^{2}),

with a remainder of absolute value at most 32​ε2​N2​(N−1)\tfrac{3}{2}\varepsilon^{2}N^{2}(N-1). For equal sizes ss this reads RU=εw​K​𝔼​W​(MSTs)+εx​(K2)​s2​g​(s)+O⁡(ε2)R_{U}=\varepsilon_{w}K\,\mathbb{E}\,W(\mathrm{MST}_{s})+\varepsilon_{x}\binom{K}{2}s^{2}g(s)+O(\varepsilon^{2}).

The pipeline is exact on the noiseless input, and its output is a function of the answers and of the order, which is independent of the answers. By Lemma 1 with per-coordinate rates (end of its proof), it suffices to compute the single-error damages. We treat within-cluster and cross-cluster errors separately, since they create false splits and false merges by different mechanisms.

Within flip on a pair e⊆Cie\subseteq C_{i}. All cross answers are correct (“different”), so no block ever contains items of two clusters, since a merge needs a “same” answer. A ≠\neq constraint between two blocks of the same cluster is created only by a query between them answered “different”, that is, only by ee. Constraints between blocks of different clusters never affect a decision on a within pair. Hence cluster CiC_{i} evolves exactly as the single-cluster pipeline under the order π\pi restricted to its pairs, which is uniform, with one flip; and the other clusters end intact. By Theorem 8 the damage is ne(si−ne) 1{e∈Tπ|Ci}n_{e}(s_{i}-n_{e})\,\mathbf{1}\{e\in T_{\pi|C_{i}}\}, where Tπ|CiT_{\pi|C_{i}} is the Kruskal tree of the restricted order. The sum of these damages over the within pairs of CiC_{i} is W⁡(Tπ|Ci)W(T_{\pi|C_{i}}), whose expectation is 𝔼​W​(MSTsi)\mathbb{E}\,W(\mathrm{MST}_{s_{i}}).

Cross flip on a pair ee between CiC_{i} and CjC_{j}. Let S=Ci∪CjS=C_{i}\cup C_{j}. We use induction over time. (a) Every block is contained in SS or disjoint from SS, and every block disjoint from SS lies inside one cluster. This holds because a merge of blocks from different clusters needs a “same” answer on a cross pair, and only e⊆Se\subseteq S has one. (b) A ≠\neq constraint between two blocks inside SS is created only by a query of a pair inside SS, and it is inherited only through merges inside SS. Pairs with an endpoint outside SS only create constraints that involve a block outside SS, or merge two blocks of one cluster outside SS; neither changes a decision on a pair inside SS. Therefore the state restricted to SS (its blocks and the constraints among them) changes only at the arrivals of pairs inside SS, as a deterministic function of their relative order, which is uniform. The clusters outside SS end intact, as in the within case without a flip, and they are separated from everything else. So the expected loss is exactly g⁡(si,sj)g(s_{i},s_{j}). Summing over the si​sjs_{i}s_{j} cross pairs between CiC_{i} and CjC_{j} gives the formula. ∎

Lemma 21 (Anatomy of one false merge).

In the two-cluster setting of gg, let τ\tau be the arrival time of ee. Let PP be the component of uu in the graph formed by the pairs inside AA that arrive before τ\tau, and let QQ be the component of vv in the graph formed by the pairs inside BB that arrive before τ\tau. Let qq denote the event that ee is queried.

  1. 1.

    (Query event.) The pair ee is queried if and only if no pair of P×QP\times Q other than ee arrives before τ\tau. Hence ℙ⁡(q∣τ,P,Q)=(1−τ)|P|​|Q|−1\mathbb{P}(q\mid\tau,P,Q)=(1-\tau)^{|P||Q|-1}. If ee is not queried, then De=0D_{e}=0.

  2. 2.

    (Final form.) If ee is queried, the final partition of A∪BA\cup B is {X,A∖XA,B∖XB}\{X,\ A\setminus X_{A},\ B\setminus X_{B}\}, with empty sets dropped. Here XX is the final block of uu, which contains uu and vv, and XA=X∩AX_{A}=X\cap A, XB=X∩BX_{B}=X\cap B. With a=|XA|a=|X_{A}| and b=|XB|b=|X_{B}|,

    De=a​b⏟FP+a⁡(sA−a)+b⁡(sB−b)⏟FN.D_{e}=\underbrace{ab}_{\mathrm{FP}}+\underbrace{a(s_{A}-a)+b(s_{B}-b)}_{\mathrm{FN}}.
  3. 3.

    (Mechanism.) After τ\tau, when a pair arrives between the current block R≠XR\neq X inside AA and the block XX, and the two blocks carry no constraint, the pair is queried. If it lies inside AA, it is answered “same” and RR joins XX. If it is a cross pair between RR and XBX_{B}, it is answered “different” (correctly), and RR, together with every block that later merges with RR, stays outside XX, because the ≠\neq constraint is inherited. The same holds with AA and BB exchanged. A ≠\neq constraint inherited from before τ\tau, created by a cross pair between RR and QQ that arrived before τ\tau, excludes RR from the start.

  4. 4.

    (Bounds on the damage.) On the query event, max⁡(sA,sB)−1≤De≤(sA+sB2)\max(s_{A},s_{B})-1\leq D_{e}\leq\binom{s_{A}+s_{B}}{2}. For sA=sB=ss_{A}=s_{B}=s, s−1≤De≤s2s-1\leq D_{e}\leq s^{2}.

Proof.

1. Before τ\tau all answers are correct. Two blocks of the same cluster never carry a constraint, because all within answers are “same”. So the blocks are the components of the within-cluster graphs of the pairs that have arrived. By induction over time, a block P′P^{\prime} inside AA and a block Q′Q^{\prime} inside BB carry a constraint if and only if some pair of P′×Q′P^{\prime}\times Q^{\prime} has arrived. Indeed, when such a pair arrives, the blocks of its two endpoints (which lie inside P′P^{\prime} and Q′Q^{\prime}) either already carry a constraint, or the pair is queried and answered “different”, which creates one; and constraints persist under merges. Conversely, a constraint is created only by a query on an arrived pair between the two blocks involved. At time τ\tau the blocks of uu and vv are PP and QQ, and ee is queried if and only if they carry no constraint. Given τ\tau and the within-cluster graphs, the |P|​|Q|−1|P||Q|-1 cross pairs of P×QP\times Q other than ee arrive before τ\tau independently, each with probability τ\tau. If ee is skipped, every accepted answer is correct, and the output is the truth.

2. After τ\tau, the only block that contains items of both clusters is XX, because no other cross answer is “same”. Two blocks inside AA and outside XX never carry a constraint against each other: such a constraint needs a query between them answered “different”, but all answers on pairs inside AA are “same”. So all items of AA outside XX end in one block, since the first arriving pair between two such blocks merges them; the same holds for BB; and XX never splits. The loss formula counts the pairs of XA×XBX_{A}\times X_{B} (wrongly together) and the pairs of XA×(A∖XA)X_{A}\times(A\setminus X_{A}) and XB×(B∖XB)X_{B}\times(B\setminus X_{B}) (wrongly apart).

3. This is the rule of the pipeline applied to the blocks RR and XX, together with the inheritance of constraints.

4. We have a,b≥1a,b\geq 1. If a<sAa<s_{A}, then a⁡(sA−a)≥sA−1a(s_{A}-a)\geq s_{A}-1; if a=sAa=s_{A}, then a​b≥sAab\geq s_{A}. In both cases De≥sA−1D_{e}\geq s_{A}-1, and the same argument gives De≥sB−1D_{e}\geq s_{B}-1. The upper bound (sA+sB2)\binom{s_{A}+s_{B}}{2} is the number of pairs. For equal sizes, a​b+a⁡(s−a)+b⁡(s−b)=s⁡(a+b)−a2−b2+a​b≤s2ab+a(s-a)+b(s-b)=s(a+b)-a^{2}-b^{2}+ab\leq s^{2}, since on [0,s]2[0,s]^{2} this concave function is maximized at a=b=sa=b=s. ∎

Proposition 23 (Limit of the query probability).

Assume (E1)–(E3). In the two-cluster setting with sA=sB=ss_{A}=s_{B}=s,

lims→∞s​ℙ​(q)=Cq:=∫0∞f⁡(c)​𝑑c,f⁡(c)={1,c≤1,(1−θc)2+2​θc​(1−θc)​𝔼​e−c​θc​K,K∼Borel⁡(μc),c>1.\lim_{s\to\infty}s\,\mathbb{P}(q)=C_{q}:=\int_{0}^{\infty}f(c)\,dc,\qquad f(c)=\begin{cases}1,&c\leq 1,\\[2.0pt] (1-\theta_{c})^{2}+2\theta_{c}(1-\theta_{c})\,\mathbb{E}\,e^{-c\theta_{c}K},\ \ K\sim\mathrm{Borel}(\mu_{c}),&c>1.\end{cases}

Proof.

By Lemma 21(1), ℙ⁡(q)=∫01ℙ⁡(q∣τ)​𝑑τ\mathbb{P}(q)=\int_{0}^{1}\mathbb{P}(q\mid\tau)\,d\tau with ℙ⁡(q∣τ)=𝔼​(1−τ)|P|​|Q|−1\mathbb{P}(q\mid\tau)=\mathbb{E}(1-\tau)^{|P||Q|-1}, where PP and QQ are independent copies of the component of a fixed vertex in G⁡(s,τ)G(s,\tau). Proof of Proposition 14.

We show that the node-ordering (pivot) pipeline of Vesdapunt et al. (2014), with KK clusters of size ss, has

Rpiv=εw​K​(s−1)2+εx​(K2)​s​(2​s−1)+O⁡(ε2).R_{\mathrm{piv}}=\varepsilon_{w}K(s-1)^{2}+\varepsilon_{x}\binom{K}{2}s(2s-1)+O(\varepsilon^{2}).

In this pipeline the items arrive in uniformly random order. A new item is compared with each existing block’s representative (its first item), following the order in which the blocks were created. It joins the first block that answers “same”; if all answers are “different”, it starts a new block.

Greedy form. Each comparison of an item with a representative settles the relation of the item to the whole block. So the pipeline is a greedy decoder on the partition code with an adaptive order. Its output is a function of the answers and of the arrival order, which is independent of the answers, and with correct answers it returns the truth. So Lemma 1, with per-coordinate rates, applies. With only one wrong answer, the run agrees with the noiseless run until that pair is compared. It therefore has the same probability of being queried as in the noiseless run.

Numbers of comparisons. Clusters are created in a uniformly random order. In the noiseless run, an item of the cluster created ρ\rho-th is compared with exactly the ρ−1\rho-1 earlier representatives before it reaches its own representative (or before it creates its cluster). Since ρ\rho is uniform on {1,…,K}\{1,\dots,K\}, the expected number of cross comparisons is n⁡(K−1)/2n(K-1)/2. Every item except the KK founders makes exactly one within comparison, so there are n−Kn-K within comparisons.

Damage of a false merge. Suppose that the only wrong answer is a false “same” between an item i∈Ai\in A and the representative of the block of another cluster BB. Then ii joins the block of BB and remains there for the rest of the run. Later items of AA are compared with representatives, never with ii, and the block of BB collects all of BB. So the damage is ss FP pairs (ii with the items of BB) plus s−1s-1 FN pairs (ii with the other items of AA), that is, 2​s−12s-1. This also holds when ii is the first item of AA: the next item of AA then creates the block of AA.

Damage of a false split. Suppose that the only wrong answer is a false “different” between an item ii and the representative of its own block. Then ii continues with the later representatives, all of which answer “different” correctly, and it creates a singleton block. Later items of its cluster meet the older representative first, receive “same”, and never reach the block of ii. So the damage is s−1s-1 FN pairs.

Summation. By Lemma 1, Rpiv=εx⋅n⁡(K−1)2⋅(2​s−1)+εw​(n−K)​(s−1)+O⁡(ε2)R_{\mathrm{piv}}=\varepsilon_{x}\cdot\frac{n(K-1)}{2}\cdot(2s-1)+\varepsilon_{w}(n-K)(s-1)+O(\varepsilon^{2}) with n=K​sn=Ks. Since n⁡(K−1)2=(K2)​s\frac{n(K-1)}{2}=\binom{K}{2}s and (n−K)​(s−1)=K​(s−1)2(n-K)(s-1)=K(s-1)^{2}, this is the claim. ∎

A.4 Pivot-based sorting

There are nn keys, which we identify with their true ranks 1,…,n1,\dots,n. The order code has one coordinate for each of the (n2)\binom{n}{2} pairs of keys, and its codewords are the n!n! total orders. The answer on a pair is its orientation, that is, which of the two keys is smaller. Each answer is wrong with probability pp, independently over the pairs. The loss is the number of pairs that the output order inverts; this is the Hamming distance on the order code. The raw decoder has risk p​(n2)p\binom{n}{2}. Randomized quicksort with noisy comparisons chooses a pivot qq uniformly at random from the current list and compares it with every other key of the list, reading the answer on each such pair. It sends each key to the left or to the right sublist according to the answer, sorts the two sublists recursively, and outputs the left sublist, the pivot and the right sublist, in this order. We write Hn=∑k=1n1/kH_{n}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}1/k for the nn-th harmonic number.

Alonso et al. (2004) established 𝔼​I​(n,p)∼n2​p\mathbb{E}I(n,p)\sim n^{2}p for quicksort with independent comparison errors in the regime n→∞n\to\infty, p→0p\to 0 and n​p→∞np\to\infty (their Theorem 2.2 and Remark 2.8). Below, we derive the exact fixed-nn first-order constant in Proposition 24 by counting single-error damage and using the classical comparison probabilities.

Proposition 24 (Quicksort).

With comparisons wrong independently with probability pp, the expected number of inversions of randomized quicksort is p⁡(n2+3​n−2​(n+1)​Hn)+O⁡(p2)p\,(n^{2}+3n-2(n+1)H_{n})+O(p^{2}), where HnH_{n} is the nn-th harmonic number; the amplification tends to 2.

Proof of Proposition 24.

We first identify randomized quicksort as a greedy decoder with an adaptive, pivot-first order. We then show that a single wrong comparison of key ii with pivot qq costs |i−q||i-q| inversions. Weighting these costs by their comparison probabilities gives

RQS(p)=p(n2+3n−2(n+1)Hn)+O(p2),n2+3​n−2​(n+1)​Hn(n2)⟶2(n→∞),R_{\mathrm{QS}}(p)=p\,\big(n^{2}+3n-2(n+1)H_{n}\big)+O(p^{2}),\qquad\frac{n^{2}+3n-2(n+1)H_{n}}{\binom{n}{2}}\longrightarrow 2\quad(n\to\infty),

so that the amplification over the raw decoder tends to 2.

Quicksort as a greedy decoder. The accepted answers compare each chosen pivot with the keys in its current sublist. They arrange the keys into a sequence of current sublists separated by pivots. Every total order that keeps this left-to-right arrangement, and orders each current sublist arbitrarily, is consistent with all answers read so far. Hence the relation between two keys of the same current sublist is not implied, and quicksort queries such a pair if one of the two keys becomes the pivot while both are still in that sublist. After a pivot qq has been compared with every key of its sublist, every pair (l,r)(l,r) with ll and rr on opposite sides of qq is implied by transitivity through qq, and it is skipped. More generally, a pair that quicksort never compares is split by some pivot that was compared with both of its keys, so its relation is implied by transitivity. Pairs inside a sublist are processed later, in the recursion. So quicksort accepts the non-implied pairs and skips the implied ones, in an adaptive order: first the pivot against the keys of its sublist, then the pairs across the two new sublists, then recursively inside each sublist. This is the greedy decoder with an adaptive pivot-first order, and its output is the unique total order consistent with all accepted answers. Pivots are selected by i.i.d. uniform priorities on the keys (the pivot of a sublist is its key of smallest priority), which are independent of the answers; the output is a function of the answers and the priorities, and with correct answers quicksort returns the true order. So Lemma 1 applies.

Damage of a single wrong comparison. Suppose that the only wrong answer is on the comparison of key ii with pivot qq, say with i<qi<q, so that ii is sent to the right sublist. All other comparisons are correct. So the right sublist, which contains the keys larger than qq together with ii, is sorted correctly, and ii becomes its minimum, placed immediately after qq. The left sublist is also sorted correctly. The inverted pairs are (i,q)(i,q) and (i,k)(i,k) for i<k<qi<k<q, that is, q−iq-i pairs. The case i>qi>q is symmetric, with i−qi-q inverted pairs. An answer on a pair that quicksort does not compare is never read, and then the damage is 0.

Probability of a comparison. In the noiseless run, the keys of ranks i<ji<j are compared if and only if one of them is the first pivot chosen among the ranks i,…,ji,\dots,j; before that, all these keys stay in one sublist. By symmetry each of these j−i+1j-i+1 keys is equally likely to be chosen first, so the probability is 2/(j−i+1)2/(j-i+1). With a single wrong answer on the pair {i,j}\{i,j\}, the run coincides with the noiseless run until this answer is read, so the pair is compared with the same probability.

First-order constant. By Lemma 1, the first-order constant is

∑i<j2j−i+1​(j−i)=n⁡(n−1)−∑i<j2j−i+1=n⁡(n−1)−[2​(n+1)​Hn−4​n]=n2+3​n−2​(n+1)​Hn.\sum_{i<j}\frac{2}{j-i+1}\,(j-i)=n(n-1)-\sum_{i<j}\frac{2}{j-i+1}=n(n-1)-\big[2(n+1)H_{n}-4n\big]=n^{2}+3n-2(n+1)H_{n}.

Here ∑i<j2j−i+1=∑k=2n2​(n+1−k)k=2​(n+1)​(Hn−1)−2​(n−1)=2​(n+1)​Hn−4​n\sum_{i<j}\frac{2}{j-i+1}=\sum_{k=2}^{n}\frac{2(n+1-k)}{k}=2(n+1)(H_{n}-1)-2(n-1)=2(n+1)H_{n}-4n, where k=j−i+1k=j-i+1 and there are n+1−kn+1-k pairs with j−i+1=kj-i+1=k. Dividing by (n2)=n⁡(n−1)/2\binom{n}{2}=n(n-1)/2 and using Hn=O⁡(log⁡n)H_{n}=O(\log n) shows that the amplification tends to 2. ∎

Appendix B Numerical validation

This appendix gives the simulation methods and results for Tables 4, 2, 7 and 2. Query orders are uniformly random unless stated otherwise. Reported uncertainties are Monte Carlo standard errors (MCSE): the sample standard deviation divided by the square root of the number of replicates. The code supplement provides the scripts, outputs and commands needed to reproduce each result; random runs use fixed seeds. Simulations run on one CPU core.

Conservation and Horn hubs.

We then run the full pipeline on K=4K=4 clusters of size 3, with independent answer errors at rate ε=10−3\varepsilon=10^{-3}. Over 200000 runs, 𝔼​FP/ε=58.1±1.1\mathbb{E}\,\mathrm{FP}/\varepsilon=58.1\pm 1.1 and 𝔼​FN/ε=71.9±1.0\mathbb{E}\,\mathrm{FN}/\varepsilon=71.9\pm 1.0. Dividing by the error rate makes these estimates comparable to the first-order coefficients: 56.8756.87 and 72.0372.03, computed from the exact gFP​(3)g_{\rm FP}(3), gFN​(3)g_{\rm FN}(3) and 𝔼​W​(MST3)=4\mathbb{E}\,W(\mathrm{MST}_{3})=4 in Theorem 12. Because these runs allow multiple errors, the normalized expectations can differ from the first-order coefficients by O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon).

Finite noise.

To test the orders when several answers may be wrong in one run, Tables 2 and 7 use one cluster with m=100m=100 or m=200m=200 records. Every answer is independently flipped to “different” with probability δ∈{0.01,0.02,0.05,0.1,0.2}\delta\in\{0.01,0.02,0.05,0.1,0.2\}. Pivot first asks all pairs {0,j}\{0,j\} involving a fixed record and then processes the remaining pairs in random order. The random order uniformly permutes all pairs. Each cell uses 200 runs, with seeds 20260929 and 20261006 for m=100m=100 and m=200m=200, respectively. All 2000 runs at m=200m=200 satisfy the loss bounds of Lemma 7.

Appendix C Real-LLM experiment

Data and model answers.

We use HPI’s 1,879-record Cora file and duplicate-pair list (Hasso Plattner Institute, n.d.). Duplicate-pair connected components define 182 entities, one per paper. Records use “field: value” pairs in the fixed order authors, title, journal, booktitle, institution, publisher, volume, pages, date and year. Qwen2.5-1.5B (base) (Qwen Team, 2024) receives six hand-written citation-pair examples (three Yes, three No; none from Cora), then the test pair with the smaller record identifier first. It answers “same” when logit⁡( Yes)>logit⁡( No)\mathrm{logit}(\texttt{ Yes})>\mathrm{logit}(\texttt{ No}). These next-token scores are used without sampling or fine-tuning. Similarity-first uses cosine similarity of normalized CLS embeddings from bge-small-en-v1.5 (Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence, 2023).

Experimental settings.

The one-entity experiment uses the 23 entities with at least 20 records: 1,266 records, sizes 21 to 238, and all 62,423 within-entity pairs. For the multi-entity experiment, we group these entities into six blocks of three or four with nearby embedding centroids, mimicking similarity blocking. This includes comparisons between records from similar but distinct entities. Each entity contributes at most 30 records; blocks contain 87 to 120 records and 36,151 pairs in total. Pivot uses the multi-entity pipeline of Proposition 14.

All query orders reuse the same saved model answers. Primary pivot and random comparisons average over 200 orders per instance. The natural/shuffled error-placement control uses 30 matched order draws. Shuffled errors are uniformly redistributed within each entity. Similarity-first randomly breaks cosine ties: once per entity in the primary comparison and 200 times per multi-entity block. Amplification divides final wrong-pair counts by wrong answers across all candidate pairs, including skipped pairs. The 95% bootstrap intervals resample entities (or blocks) with model answers fixed.

One-entity results.

At threshold 0, final wrong-pair fractions are 8.1% for pivot, 15.3% for random order and 5.7% for similarity-first. Pivot reduces this fraction by 7.27.2 percentage points relative to random order (pivot-minus-random interval [−18.7,−1.4][-18.7,-1.4]). Similarity-first’s lower point estimate differs from pivot by −2.5-2.5 points, with interval [−9.6,6.0][-9.6,6.0] including zero. Table 8 varies the Yes–No score-difference threshold to change the answer-error rate. At every tested rate, the pivot-minus-random interval lies below zero. In the error-placement control of Table 3, the 30 matched draws give natural-placement amplifications of 1.37 (pivot), 2.19 (random) and 0.85 (similarity-first).

Multi-entity results.

Across the six blocks, the model gives 1,444 wrong “same” answers and 846 wrong “different” answers. The final wrong-pair counts are 2,603 for pivot, 3,347 for random order and 2,759 for similarity-first. The pivot-minus-random loss-fraction difference is −2.1-2.1 percentage points, with interval [−3.4,−0.7][-3.4,-0.7]. Similarity-first produces the most false merges: 1,727 wrongly merged pairs, compared with 1,414 for pivot. Its priority for similar pairs also brings similar cross-entity pairs forward.

Exploratory runs with SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct gave almost exclusively “different” answers and the same loss for all orders. DBLP–ACM entities contain only two records, leaving no within-entity propagation to compare. These runs are not used in the reported comparisons.

Assets.
